about: The Daily's 'I didn't know that' pool. Every entry carries the source's name, a link a reader can open, the date the source was read, and the source's own words the fact rests on. An entry without them is never shown (scripts/daily_fact.py, test/daily-email-v2.test.mjs). The old quote pool (data/quote-pool.json) stays off. Each entry has one category from the list in scripts/daily_fact.py (CATEGORIES); the day's pick comes from a fixed schedule that never repeats a fact until the pool is used up and never shows one category two days running. New entries come in with scripts/daily_fact.py --import, which stamps the day they may first show ('added') so the days already sent never change.

facts.quote: USDA predicted substantial crop losses and President Reagan signed a $3.9 billion disaster relief bill for farmers in August of 1988. The relief was among an estimated $20 billion spent to help farmers.

facts.fact: The Farmers' Home Administration Act of 1946 replaced the New Deal's Farm Security Administration with a new farm lending agency.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Reviewing the History and Development of USDA Farm Loans, Part 2: 1937 to 1946 (2021)
facts.quote: The Farmers’ Home Administration Act of 1946 created a new agency to replace the FSA.

facts.fact: Ethanol went from 6% of US corn use in 2000 to 40% in 2010. A 2022 farmdoc daily article says that since 2011 it has been almost constant at 5.2 billion bushels.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Impact of Long-Run Declines in Gasoline Use on the US Corn Market (2022)
facts.quote: After 2000, the ethanol market expanded rapidly, going from 6% of corn use in 2000 to 40% in 2010. ... Since 2011, corn use for ethanol has been almost constant at 5.2 billion bushels.

facts.fact: The typical US gasoline mixture is 10% ethanol, and in 2022, 94% of US ethanol production used corn grain.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Impact of Long-Run Declines in Gasoline Use on the US Corn Market (2022)
facts.quote: Nearly all US gasoline contains ethanol as an oxygenate, with the typical mixture begin 10% ethanol and 90% gasoline. ... Corn is the U.S.’s primary raw material for ethanol production, and 94% of ethanol production uses corn grain (EIA 2022).

facts.fact: US pigs per litter grew 0.105 pigs a year from 1993 to 2022, about 37.9 percent over the 30 years.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Long-Term Trends in Pigs per Litter (2023)
facts.quote: The annual growth rate in pigs per litter was 0.105 pigs or 1.1 percent per year. This may seem small, however, over the 30-year period, this equates to an increase of 3.15 pigs per litter or an increase of approximately 37.9 percent over the 1993 to 2022 period.

facts.fact: Pounds of pork produced per US sow rose from 1,979 in 1993 to 3,314 in 2021, while the sow herd barely grew.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Long-Term Trends in Pigs per Litter (2023)
facts.quote: The annual growth rate in the U.S. sow herd during the 1993 to 2022 period is only 0.15 percent per year. ... In terms of per sow production, pounds produced per sow increased from 1,979 in 1993 to 3,314 in 2021.

facts.fact: In 34 years at the University of Nebraska, wheat breeder Stephen Baenziger released or co-released 42 wheat varieties.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, To All the Wheats That I Have Known (2020)
facts.quote: I came in June 1986 and in the following 34 years have released or co-released 42 wheat cultivars with 2 additional ones pending.

facts.fact: US tractor makers began putting rollover protection on all tractors over 20 horsepower in 1986. A 2023 University of Nebraska article says many tractors made before 1986 are still widely used and unlikely to have been retrofitted.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Older Tractors Still a Danger in Agriculture (2023)
facts.quote: Beginning in 1986, American tractor manufacturers began voluntarily adding ROPS (Roll Over Protection Structure) on all farm tractors sold in the United States over 20 horsepower. ... Many tractors manufactured before 1986 are still widely used on farms and unlikely to have been retrofitted with ROPS.

facts.fact: A 2023 University of Nebraska article says tractor overturns are the leading cause of fatal farm injuries in the US, averaging about 130 deaths a year. One operator in 10 overturns a tractor in a lifetime.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Older Tractors Still a Danger in Agriculture (2023)
facts.quote: Tractor overturns are the leading cause of fatal injuries on U.S. farms, resulting in an average of about 130 deaths each year. One in 10 operators overturns a tractor in his or her lifetime.

facts.fact: In 2022, at least 42 grain bin entrapments were reported in Nebraska, the most in a decade.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Safety Takes Center Stage (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, at least 42 grain bin entrapments were reported in Nebraska, the highest in a decade.

facts.fact: Purdue counted more than 900 grain engulfments in the US over 50 years, and 62% of them were fatal.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Engulfment: Quicksand of the Midwest (2016)
facts.quote: Purdue University reported more than 900 cases of grain engulfment nationally and a fatality rate of 62% in the past 50 years.

facts.fact: Freeing a person buried to the waist in grain takes force equal to their body weight plus 600 pounds. Fully buried, it can exceed 2,000 pounds.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Engulfment: Quicksand of the Midwest (2016)
facts.quote: A person buried to the waist in grain requires a force equivalent to his/her own body weight plus 600 pounds to be freed. The force required to remove a person buried under grain can exceed 2,000 pounds.

facts.fact: Northern Great Plains soils are only 11,000 to 14,000 years old, yet hold some of the highest organic matter of any US mineral soils, 4% to 7%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soil Organic Matter and Its Benefits (2017)
facts.quote: Soils of the Northern Great Plains are relatively young (11,000 to 14,000 years old) and have some of the highest organic matter levels (4% to 7%) of all mineral soils in the United States

facts.fact: Soil microbes need 25 to 30 parts carbon for each part nitrogen. Residue above 30:1 breaks down slowly; below 20:1, nitrogen is lost.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soil Organic Matter and Its Benefits (2017)
facts.quote: On average microorganisms require 25 to 30 parts of carbon for every part of nitrogen they consume. Therefore, high C:N ratios above 30:1 will result in slower decomposition rates, whereas, low C:N ratios below 20:1 will result in nitrogen losses.

facts.fact: 2024 was Nebraska's second warmest year on record at 52.7°F, behind only 2012 at 54.0°F.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, 2024 Was the Second Warmest Year on Record in Nebraska
facts.quote: Official statewide average temperature for the year comes in at 52.7°F. This puts 2024 as the second warmest all-time in Nebraska, behind only 54.0°F in 2012.

facts.fact: Norfolk, Nebraska, fell from 75°F to 15°F between Feb. 26 and 27, 2024, a new all-time temperature drop for the town.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, February 2024 Climate Summary
facts.quote: For Norfolk, the drop from 75°F to 15°F between the 1556 CST observations on Feb. 26 and 27 was a new all-time temperature drop.
facts.note: The year comes from the page title, February 2024 Climate Summary.

facts.fact: February 2024 averaged 38.4°F in Nebraska, 11.7°F above normal. Only February 1954, at 40.2°F, was warmer.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, February 2024 Climate Summary
facts.quote: The statewide average temperature of 38.4°F in February 2024 was 11.7°F above average and made it the second-warmest February on record in Nebraska, cooler only than February 1954 (40.2°F).

facts.fact: As of June 2024, Nebraska's warmest June on record was June 1933, at a statewide 76.6°F.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, June 2024 Climate Summary
facts.quote: Temperatures were well-shy of record levels at the state level (record warmest was 76.6°F in 1933).

facts.fact: A 2022 University of Nebraska summary said that for the past three decades, June in Nebraska had warmed by nearly 4°F in the average monthly temperature.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, June Ranks in Top 10 Driest on Record for Nebraska (2022)
facts.quote: For the past three decades, Nebraska has gotten hotter in June, with an increase of nearly 4°F in the average monthly temperatures.

facts.fact: On June 7, 2022, storm spotters filed 89 hail reports and 74 wind reports across Nebraska in one day.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, June Ranks in Top 10 Driest on Record for Nebraska (2022)
facts.quote: Widespread severe weather was reported on June 7 when 89 hail and 74 wind reports were issued by storm spotters
facts.note: The year comes from the article, a summary of June 2022 published that year.

facts.fact: Sorghum ergot turned up in Nebraska fields in 2026 for the first time since 2014. It favors 50 to 55°F nights around flowering.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Sorghum Ergot in Nebraska May Lead to Harvest Challenges
facts.quote: A rare disease is showing up in Nebraska sorghum fields for the first time since 2014 ... Infection is favored when nighttime temperatures are 50°–55°F during pollen formation (two-three weeks prior to flowering) and at flowering
facts.note: 2026 is the year of the article, which reports the find in the current season.

facts.fact: A car at 65 mph closes on a combine half a mile ahead going 15 mph in just 36 seconds.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Staying Safe During Harvest (2022)
facts.quote: if a vehicle is traveling 65 mph, and a combine is half of a mile ahead and traveling at 15 mph in the same direction, it would take 36 seconds for your vehicle to meet the combine.

facts.fact: USDA counted over 890 million bushels of corn stored on Nebraska farms in 2023, up 31% from 2022.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Safety Takes Center Stage (2024)
facts.quote: According to the USDA NASS report in 2023, there were over 890 million bushels of corn stored on Nebraska farms, an increase of 31% from 2022.

facts.fact: At one time there were over 75 companies making center pivot and lateral move irrigation systems.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Center Pivots: Innovation That Grew Crops and Acres in Nebraska (2024)
facts.quote: There were once over 75 center pivot/lateral move irrigation manufacturers.

facts.fact: The 2007 Census of Agriculture showed Nebraska passing California for the most irrigated farmland, about one of every six irrigated acres in the US.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Leads the Nation in Irrigated Acres
facts.quote: The most recent U.S. 2007 Census of Agriculture, released in February, shows Nebraska now has more irrigated farmland acres than any other state, accounting for about one of every six acres of U.S. irrigated farmland. ... California, which historically has been first in irrigated acres

facts.fact: An estimated 52,000 center pivots were running in Nebraska in 2005, and every one of the state's 93 counties has some irrigation.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Leads the Nation in Irrigated Acres
facts.quote: In 2005, an estimated 52,000 center-pivot systems operated in Nebraska, and that number has only increased, he said. There is some irrigation in each of the state's 93 counties.

facts.fact: Texas cut irrigation on about 750,000 acres from 1997 to 2007 as the Ogallala Aquifer dropped from overuse.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Leads the Nation in Irrigated Acres
facts.quote: Texas, which shares part of the vast Ogallala Aquifer with Nebraska, reduced irrigation on about 750,000 acres between 1997 and 2007 as aquifer levels have declined due to overuse.

facts.fact: Nebraska grows more Great Northern beans than any other state. Its 2023 dry bean crop brought $82.4 million from 92,000 acres.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Dry Beans
facts.quote: In 2023, Nebraska's dry edible beans production resulted in $82.4 million from 92,000 acres harvested, according to USDA National Agricultural Statistics Service. Nebraska ranks 1st in production of Great Northern beans.

facts.fact: In 2024, Nebraska was number one in the nation for beef and veal exports, at $2,039,768,864.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Agriculture is Amazing! Celebrate National Ag Week March 16-22
facts.quote: Last year, Nebraska beef and veal exports reached a milestone, surpassing the $2 billion-mark. At $2,039,768,864, Nebraska is number one in the nation for beef and veal exports.
facts.note: The page is dated March 14, 2025 and says 'Last year', so the year is 2024.

facts.fact: As of March 2025, Nebraska was home to 24 ethanol plants with a capacity over 2.3 billion gallons a year, second largest in the nation.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Agriculture is Amazing! Celebrate National Ag Week March 16-22
facts.quote: For example, our state is home to 24 ethanol plants with a production capacity exceeding 2.3 billion gallons annually, making us the secondlargest ethanol producer in the nation.
facts.note: The page is dated March 14, 2025.

facts.fact: Combine exhaust parts and turbochargers can reach 1,000 to 1,200°F. Crop residue can catch fire at about 500°F.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Preventing and Responding to Combine Fires
facts.quote: The exhaust components and turbochargers can reach 1,000-1,200oF, with surface temperatures reaching around 900oF. Crop residues have been reported to ignite at approximately 500oF and above.

facts.fact: In one study, 48.5% of combine fires started between 2 and 4 p.m., when it is hottest and humidity is lowest.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Preventing and Responding to Combine Fires
facts.quote: A study conducted by Venem, M.T., et al found that 48.5% of combine fires occurred between 2 p.m. and 4 p.m. when temperatures have peaked, and relative humidity is the lowest.

facts.fact: A Spanish study in 2018 and 2019 found bearings and belts caused 18% of combine fires. A bearing over 300°F means shut the machine off now.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Preventing and Responding to Combine Fires
facts.quote: A study out of Spain conducted in 2018 and 2019 found that bearings and belts caused 18% of combine fires. ... If bearing reach temperatures above 300oF, shut the machine off immediately.

facts.fact: Combine and tractor fires cause over $20 million in US property losses a year and 40 to 50 serious injuries.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Keeping Your Equipment and Fields Fire Safe At Harvest (2017)
facts.quote: The National Ag Safety Database estimates that combine and tractor fires cause over $20 million in property losses annually in the US ... Combine and tractor fires also cause 40-50 serious injuries each year.

facts.fact: By 2017 there were 480 unique cases of herbicide-resistant weeds worldwide, across 252 weed species.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Status of Herbicide-Resistant Weeds in Nebraska (2017)
facts.quote: There are 480 unique cases of herbicide-resistant weed biotypes globally in 252 weed species (147 dicots and 105 monocots).
facts.note: 2017 is the year of the article, dated March 2017 on the page.

facts.fact: Nebraska grew 2.02 billion bushels of corn in 2025 at 194 bushels an acre, and soybeans averaged 65.5 bushels.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska 2025 Annual Crop Production Summary
facts.quote: Nebraska’s 2025 crop production reflected a year of contrasts ... Corn for grain production in Nebraska based on year-end surveys is estimated at 2.02 billion bushels, up 12% from 2024 ... Yield of 194 bushels per acre is up 6 bushels from last year. ... Yield, at 65.5 bushels per acre, is up 8 bushels from a year earlier.

facts.fact: Western bean cutworm moths lay eggs in clusters of 5 to 200 on the top of a corn plant's uppermost leaf. Flight usually peaks July 10 to 24.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Scouting and Treating Western Bean Cutworm
facts.quote: Western bean cutworm moths lay eggs in clusters of five to 200 on the top surface of the upper most leaf of a corn plant and on any leaf surface of dry beans. ... The moth flight usually peaks between July 10 and July 24.
facts.note: five is written as 5.

facts.fact: It usually takes an average of 5 to 10 corn rootworm beetles per ear to seriously hurt pollination.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Time to Scout for Western Corn Rootworm Beetles (2017)
facts.quote: Usually an average of 5-10 beetles per ear is required to seriously affect pollination.

facts.fact: Nebraska's sugarbeet industry began in 1890 with the first factory at Grand Island. Leaf spot later pushed it west to the Panhandle.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Sugarbeets
facts.quote: Sugarbeet production in Nebraska began in 1890, with the first factory being established in Grand Island. Production moved into western Nebraska and the Panhandle early in the 20th Century, due in large part because of increasingly severe problems with Cercospora leaf spot.

facts.fact: The Great Western Sugar Company brought sugar to Colorado in 1901. Its growers formed the Western Sugar Cooperative in December 2002, with more than 1,000 members.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Sugarbeets
facts.quote: The Great Western Sugar Company brought the sugar industry into Colorado in 1901 before expanding into Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana. After undergoing several different changes of ownership, the Western Sugar Cooperative was formed in December of 2002 consisting of more than 1,000 growers in Colorado, Nebraska, Wyoming and Montana.

facts.fact: From 1978 to 1998, Americans cut what they spent on beef per person by half after inflation and still got 78% as much beef.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Consumer Spending and Beef Demand (2012)
facts.quote: Figure 1 shows that the average amount that each consumer spent on beef, on an inflation-adjusted basis, tumbled by more than 50% in the 20-year period between 1978 and 1998. Spending collapsed from $539.15 per person to $260.25 per person, all in 2011 dollars, and the amounts purchased slid from 87.5 pounds per person to 68.1 pounds per person, all on a retail-weight basis. It’s clear that the industry had a serious demand problem during this period, because consumers were able to cut spending by one-half on an inflation-adjusted basis and still receive 78% as much product.
facts.note: 1978 to 1998 is the period the article gives for its Figure 1.

facts.fact: From 1998 to 2004, Americans paid more for less beef, a sign of stronger demand. The high point came in 2004, the year right after the December 2003 BSE discovery.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Consumer Spending and Beef Demand (2012)
facts.quote: Per capita expenditures recovered through 2004 ... Between 1998 and 2004, consumers spent more inflation-adjusted dollars ($60.15) for less beef (1.9 pounds) – a textbook example of stronger demand. Even more remarkable is the fact that the high point occurred in the calendar year immediately following the December 2003 BSE discovery.

facts.fact: After the Soviet breakup, Kazakhstan, Russia and Ukraine went from 3% to 12% of world grain exports, while the U.S. share fell from 41% to 31%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Kazakhstan, Russia, Ukraine (KRU) and World Grain Markets (2012)
facts.quote: The corresponding increase in KRU’s average share of world grain exports was from 3% to 12%. In comparison for the same periods, the U.S. average share of world wheat exports declined from 31% to 20% while the U.S. average share of world grain exports declined from 41% to 31%.

facts.fact: USDA's wheat feed and residual use, mostly livestock feed, ranged from 16 million bushels, a 0.7% share of total wheat use, in the 2007 crop year to 484 million bushels, a 19.9% share, in 1990.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Wheat Feeding (2012)
facts.quote: The specific use category is “feed and residual.’ Thus, this use category is best thought of as “use mostly for livestock feed.” ... Wheat Feeding as a Share of Total Wheat Use ... Wheat feeding has ranged from 16 million bushels or a 0.7% share in the 2007 wheat crop year to 484 million bushels or a 19.9% share in the 1990 wheat crop year.
facts.note: The wheat crop year runs June 1 to May 31; the article refers to a crop year by its first year.

facts.fact: In USDA's wheat feed and residual data for 1974 to 2011, 15% more wheat was reported fed in June to August than in the whole year. The article calls this a data reporting relationship that reflects residual use.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Wheat Feeding (2012)
facts.quote: The wheat crop year runs from June 1 through May 31. ... In fact, between the 1974 and 2011 crop years, USDA reports that 15% more wheat was fed during the first quarter than was fed for the entire year. While not possible if the use category was only feeding, this data reporting relationship serves as a reminder of the important role residual use plays in this use category.

facts.fact: In 2010, about 56% of US farmland was farmed by its owner, but only 41% in Illinois. Share rent covered 18% of Illinois acres against 7% nationally.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Tenure in the USA and in Illinois (2013)
facts.quote: In 2010, the USDA collected detailed information on land tenure ... Thus, the majority of acreage in the United States is owner-operated, at approximately 56%. ... In contrast, only 41% of farmland acreage in Illinois is owner-operated. ... In addition, share rental agreements account for a larger portion of Illinois farmland acreage (18%) than for United States as a whole (7%).

facts.fact: In early 2013, after the 2012 drought, US cattle numbers fell to their lowest since 1952 and beef cows to their lowest since 1962.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Where Have All the Beef Cows Gone? (2013)
facts.quote: Cattle numbers are down again, to their lowest level since 1952, according to USDA’s recent inventory count. Beef cow numbers are at their lowest level since 1962 as the devastating impacts of the 2012 drought continues the longer-term decline.
facts.note: 2013 is the year of the article (February 2013), which reports USDA's January inventory.

facts.fact: From 2007 to 2012 the US beef cow herd dropped 3.6 million head, 11 percent. The Northern Plains was the only region that grew.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Where Have All the Beef Cows Gone? (2013)
facts.quote: The 2012 drought was just the latest event to result in the liquidation of cows that has been accelerating since 2007. Nationally, the beef cow herd has dropped by 3.6 million head (11 percent) with reductions in all regions except the Northern Plains.

facts.fact: Illinois farmland prices rose 21.4 percent in 2011, the biggest one-year jump in over three decades.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, A Historical Perspective on Illinois Farmland Sales (2013)
facts.quote: In 2011, Illinois farmland prices increased 21.4 percent, the largest single-year jump in over three decades.

facts.fact: After peaking in 1981, Illinois farmland prices fell 8.7 percent a year, compounded, until bottoming in 1987.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, A Historical Perspective on Illinois Farmland Sales (2013)
facts.quote: After peaking in 1981, Illinois farmland prices declined at an annually compounded rate of 8.7 percent through 1987.

facts.fact: Retail beef averaged $5.29 a pound in 2013, then hit a record $5.55 in the first quarter of 2014.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, How Did Cattle Prices Get So High? (2014)
facts.quote: In 2013, retail beef prices averaged $5.29 per pound but moved to a record $5.55 in the first quarter of 2014.

facts.fact: A study of over 10,000 Illinois farmland sales from 2001 to 2009 found big cities lift farmland prices as far as 33 miles beyond their edge.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Impact of Urban Areas on Farmland Prices in Illinois (2014)
facts.quote: By examining data from over 10,000 transactions between 2001 and 2009, the study suggested that the large urban centers influence farmland prices as far as 33 miles beyond their boundary.

facts.fact: The inability to refute rumors of massive PED death losses contributed to live hog prices overshooting to a record $76 per hundredweight average in 2014. Production fell only 2%, and by early 2015 live hogs were near $45.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Pork's Boom and Bust Price Pattern (2015)
facts.quote: A year-ago in March, the new PED virus was the talk in the livestock media. ... In recent weeks, live hog prices reached five year lows near $45 per live hundredweight, a price bust from record highs a year earlier. ... The inability to refute the rumors of massive death losses a year-ago contributed to prices overshooting to the upside. The reality that pork production was only down two percent in 2014 ... down from the extraordinary record of $76 in 2014 (previous record was $66 in 2011).
facts.note: two percent is written as 2%; 2015 is the year of the article (March 2015).

facts.fact: From 1980 to 2013, animal protein eaten per person rose 426% in China but 82% in India.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, China, India, the Food Transition, and Future Demand Growth (2015)
facts.quote: Between 1980 and 2013, per capita consumption of animal protein increased by 82% in India but by 426% in China while per capita caloric intake increased by 23% in India vs. 44% in China.

facts.fact: Across countries in 2011, food use per person leveled off around 3,000 calories and 50 grams of animal protein a day, no matter how much richer people got.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, China, India, the Food Transition, and Future Demand Growth (2015)
facts.quote: The cross sections for 2011 calories and animal protein consumed per capita per day are presented in Figures 1 and 2, respectively. ... In 2011, the plateaus occur around 3,000 calories per day and 50 grams of protein per day.

facts.fact: In 2014 Illinois led the nation in total farm rent paid, $3.8 billion.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Ownership in Illinois: New Highlights from USDA Survey (2015)
facts.quote: The USDA recently released the results of the 2014 Tenure, Ownership, and Transition of Agricultural Land (TOTAL). ... One of the most striking findings of the survey is that Illinois leads the nation in total agricultural rent at $3.8 billion.

facts.fact: Illinois had 131,337 farmland landlords in 2014, and only 15,684 of them farmed themselves.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Ownership in Illinois: New Highlights from USDA Survey (2015)
facts.quote: Illinois, for example, had 131,337 total landlords in 2014, only 15,684 of which are farm operators.

facts.fact: Trusts are the second most common kind of Illinois farm landlord, 18.2% of them in 2014, after individuals at 46.8%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Ownership in Illinois: New Highlights from USDA Survey (2015)
facts.quote: The non-operator landlords are further classified by five ownership types, the most common of which is individual ownership, accounting for 46.8% of all landlords in Illinois. Trusts were the second most common ownership arrangement at 18.2% of all landlords.
facts.note: 2014 is the survey year named on the page.

facts.fact: Wheat output in Kazakhstan, Russia and Ukraine swings more than any other big crop region's, 27% a year on average. US corn is next at 21%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Variability in Corn, Soybean, and Wheat Production across the Globe (2015)
facts.quote: Moreover, variability of wheat production in Kazakhstan-Russia-Ukraine (27%) is higher than for any other crop-country group combination. The next highest variability of production is Canada-U.S. corn at 21%.

facts.fact: After inflation, the cash cost of growing a bushel of corn in 2010-2014 was 42% lower than in 1975-1979. Soybeans were 44% lower and wheat 37%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Declining Real Cash Cost of Producing Corn, Soybean, and Wheat (2015)
facts.quote: Comparing 2010-2014 with 1975-1979, real cash cost per bushel is 42%, 44%, and 37% lower for corn, soybeans, and wheat, respectively.

facts.fact: The world's average corn yield topped 85 bushels an acre every year from 2013 to 2016. The earlier global high was 83.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, IFES 2016: Long-Term Weather and Prospects for a Recovery in Corn Prices (2017)
facts.quote: In fact, the global average corn yield exceeded 85 bushels per acre in each year over 2013-2016. The previous high yield on a global basis was 83 bushels.

facts.fact: US farmers harvested 69% of their planted oat acres in 1978-1982, but only 36% in 2013-2017.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Long Term Relationship between Yield and Acres of U.S. Field Crops (2017)
facts.quote: Harvested acres and yield per harvested acre are used for oats because share of planted oats acres harvested has declined from 69% in 1978-1982 to 36% in 2013-2017, or by 33 percentage points.

facts.fact: The 4 crops whose yields grew slowest since 1978, oats, barley, sorghum and wheat, each lost at least 30% of their planted acres by 2013-17.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Long Term Relationship between Yield and Acres of U.S. Field Crops (2017)
facts.quote: In contrast, planted acres declined by at least 30% for the 4 crops with the lowest growth in yield (oats, barley, sorghum, wheat). ... A strong positive relationship is found between the increase in yield and change in planted acres since 1978
facts.note: 2013-17 is the comparison period named on the page.

facts.fact: Over 52 years, US corn yield beat trend in 60% of years. But misses ran bigger: 8.6 bushels below on average against 5.8 above, with the worst 29.1 below in 1988.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Historic Pattern of U.S Corn Yields, Any Implications for 2012? (2012)
facts.quote: Over the 52 year period, the average yield was above the trend yield in 60 percent of the years and below the trend in 40 percent of the years. ... Specifically, the average deviation below trend was 8.6 bushels while the average deviation above trend was 5.8 bushels. The largest deviation below trend was 29.1 bushels (1988)

facts.fact: The longest run of above-trend US corn yields in the 52 years to 2011 was 7 years, 2003 to 2009.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Historic Pattern of U.S Corn Yields, Any Implications for 2012? (2012)
facts.quote: The longest run of negative deviations was 4 years (1974-1977), while positive deviations had runs of 4 years (1984-1987), 5 years (1965-1969), and 7 years (2003–2009).
facts.note: 52 years to 2011: the article's sample is the 52 years before its February 2012 date.

facts.fact: US wheat exports averaged 41 million metric tons a year in 1981-1985 but only 27 million in 2018-2022.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, US Feed Grain, Oilseed, and Food Grain Land since 1980 (2022)
facts.quote: In contrast, use of US wheat has declined following a linear trend as US exports have declined from an average of 41 million metric tons in 1981-1985 to 27 million metric tons in 2018-2022.

facts.fact: US oilseed exports rose from 23 to 55 million metric tons a year between 1981-1985 and 2018-2022, and home use nearly doubled too.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, US Feed Grain, Oilseed, and Food Grain Land since 1980 (2022)
facts.quote: In comparison, average US domestic consumption of both feed grains and oilseeds nearly doubled, increasing from 161 to 319 million metric tons for feed grains and from 37 to 72 million metric tons for oilseeds. US exports increased from 52 to 63 million metric tons for feed grains and from 23 to 55 million metric tons for oilseeds.
facts.note: The periods 1981-1985 and 2018-2022 are the ones the page compares throughout.

facts.fact: On northern Illinois grain farms from 2013 to 2022, corn never took less than 54.7% of tillable land, and peaked at 65.9% in 2013. Wheat stayed under 1%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Historical Cropping Patterns on Illinois Grain Farms (2023)
facts.quote: During the 2013 through 2022 time period, at least 54.7 percent of the tillable land in these farms each year has been in corn. The highest was 65.9 percent in 2013 and the lowest was 54.7 percent in 2019. ... Less than 1 percent of the tillable land on these farms in any year has been planted to wheat.

facts.fact: University of Nebraska-Lincoln, citing central Great Plains research, lists grain sorghum's advantages over corn under certain conditions, including a 50% higher yield in similar dryland crop rotations.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Sorghum Research in Western Nebraska (2019)
facts.quote: However, research completed on grain sorghum in the central Great Plains region makes a compelling case for grain sorghum. It offers several advantages over corn under certain conditions: ... A 50% higher yield than corn in similar dryland crop rotations (Schlegel et al., 2019).

facts.fact: In cool western Nebraska, grain sorghum can reach mid-bloom as much as 20 days later than seed companies list.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Sorghum Research in Western Nebraska (2019)
facts.quote: Keep in mind that in our cooler environments, days to mid-bloom can be delayed by as much as 20 days when compared to what is reported by companies.

facts.fact: Wheat stem sawfly was first noted in Nebraska winter wheat in the 1990s. Lodging on field edges has since reached 100 feet, with losses of 30% to 50% in badly lodged fields.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Wheat Stem Sawfly Infestations Continue to Impact Western Nebraska
facts.quote: Yield losses in seriously lodged fields can range from 30% to 50%. ... Prior to 2013 the serious border lodging may have been 20 or 30 feet, but in the last couple years growers have reported severe lodging up to 100 feet on field margins. ... Wheat stem sawfly infesting winter wheat was first noted in Nebraska in the early to mid 1990s.

facts.fact: The wheat mosaic complex is 3 mite-spread viruses. In May 2025 surveys it turned up in every south-central and southeast Nebraska field checked.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Mosaic Virus Complex Emerges as Leading Threat to Wheat in 2025
facts.quote: Wheat disease surveys were conducted in south-central and southeast Nebraska on May 7. ... The complex consists of three viruses (WSMV, Triticum mosaic virus [TriMV] and High Plains wheat mosaic virus [HPWMoV]) and it was found in every field visited from trace levels to 100% incidence and severity.
facts.note: three is written as 3; the mite carrier is named on the page ("the mite source was a large area of volunteer wheat").

facts.fact: An average soybean crop takes up 315 pounds of nitrogen an acre, about 190 of it into the seed. Most studies find 50% to 60% comes from fixation.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Check Soybean Nodulation to Determine Inoculant Efficacy (2013)
facts.quote: On average, a soybean crop needs 315 lb N per acre, about 60% of which (190 lb) goes to seed production and 40% (125 lb) goes to stover and roots. ... Most studies show that btween 50% and 60% of the nitrogen is from N fixation.

facts.fact: Soybeans absorb about 4.8 pounds of nitrogen per bushel, so an 80-bushel crop needs about 384 pounds an acre. 60% of it is taken up after pod set begins.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Is Soybean Yield Limited by Nitrogen Supply? (2018)
facts.quote: On average, soybean needs to absorb 4.8 lbs of N per bushel produced. ... In contrast, a well-managed, irrigated crop that produces 80 bu/ac will need about 384 lbs N per acre. ... First, soybean absorbs 60% of the N after R3 (beginning of pod setting)

facts.fact: A 70-bushel soybean crop takes up about 330 pounds of nitrogen an acre above ground, about what a 245-bushel corn crop needs.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soybean Inoculation: When, Where, and Why
facts.quote: A 70 bushel per acre soybean crop will take up roughly 330 lb N/acre in the aboveground portion of the plant, roughly equivalent to the nitrogen demand of a 245 bushel per acre corn crop.

facts.fact: Where soybeans had never been grown, a 1984 Nebraska measurement found yield responses to inoculation of 49 bushels an acre. An eight-year multistate test (2000 to 2008) of 51 products averaged 0 bushels an acre.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soybean Inoculation: When, Where, and Why
facts.quote: In situations where soybeans have never been grown, yield responses of 49 bushels per acre have been measured in Nebraska (Elmore 1984). ... An eight-year study (2000-2008) testing 51 inoculant products in 73 experiments conducted in Wisconsin, Iowa, Indiana, Minnesota, and Nebraska resulted in average yield response of 0 bu/ac (De Bruin 2008).
facts.note: The multistate study is described as testing fields generally; the page sets it against the never-grown-soybeans case.

facts.fact: Soybean nodule bacteria are still in the soil after 30 years in grass, just in smaller numbers.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soybean Inoculation: When, Where, and Why
facts.quote: These bacteria are still present in soils after 30 years in grass production, just at a much lower population.

facts.fact: Japanese beetles were first found in the US in a New Jersey nursery in 1916, likely in iris bulbs. By 2015 they were in 34 states and feed on over 300 plant species.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Nebraska Extension Pest of the Month: Japanese Beetle (2017)
facts.quote: This pest was first found in the United States in a New Jersey nursery in 1916 and was likely introduced in infested iris bulbs from Japan. ... As of January of 2015, Japanese beetle has been found in 34 states in the United States. ... As adults, Japanese beetles feed on over 300 species of plants

facts.fact: Japanese beetles were found on a golf course in Crete, Nebraska, in 1994. The first report of them injuring a Nebraska field crop came in July 2011.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Japanese Beetles Reported for First Time in Nebraska Field Crops (2011)
facts.quote: Japanese Beetles Reported for First Time in Nebraska Field Crops - UNL CropWatch, July 19, 2011 ... Japanese beetles were reported previously in 1994 on turf in Crete at the Country Club.

facts.fact: A few hours at 31°F will kill corn and soybean leaves. A few minutes at 28°F can kill the whole plant, stalk and all.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Premature Frost Damage to Crops (2022)
facts.quote: Temperatures at 31°F for a few hours will kill leaves, while temperatures at 28°F for a few minutes can kill the plant, including the stalk of corn and soybean.

facts.fact: It takes four hours at 24°F or colder to freeze the growing point of alfalfa. Sorghum dies at 26°F.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Premature Frost Damage to Crops (2022)
facts.quote: Four hours at 24°F or lower will freeze the growing point at the top of alfalfa. Temperatures down to 26°F will kill milo (sorghum) and sorghum species used for grazing.

facts.fact: Nebraska's average first hard freeze runs Oct. 1-10 in the far north and Panhandle, but Oct. 17-24 in the far south and southeast.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Corn Maturity & Freeze Dates
facts.quote: Oct. 1-10 for extreme northern Nebraska and the Panhandle ... October 17-24 for extreme southern Nebraska and the southeast corner of the state.

facts.fact: A University of Nebraska tillage study has run since 1981 at Rogers Memorial Farm, 10 miles east of Lincoln.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Yields From a Long-term Tillage Comparison Study
facts.quote: A tillage study was established in 1981 at the University of Nebraska Rogers Memorial Farm (RMF), 10 miles east of Lincoln, to gain experience with various tillage systems.

facts.fact: After 16 years of grazing corn residue in a Nebraska study, soil organic matter, N, P and K were unchanged, and soil microbes had increased.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Studies Show Minimal Soil Compaction With Winter Grazing (2017)
facts.quote: After 16 years of grazing corn residue, an increase in the soil microbial community was observed (when compared to areas that were not grazed). ... After 16 years of grazing, no differences in soil organic matter, N, P or K were measured.

facts.fact: Nebraska's guide for grazing corn stalks is one cow for one month per 100 bushels of corn grown, which removes only about 15% of the residue.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Studies Show Minimal Soil Compaction With Winter Grazing (2017)
facts.quote: Grazing only removes a small percentage of residue (target 15%) and thus cover is maintained and erosion risk is not substantially increased. ... when grazed at the University's recommended rate of one cow for one month for every 100 bushels of corn grain produced.

facts.fact: A May 2025 University of Nebraska analysis found Falls City had not dropped below 28°F after May 1 since 1944. In Valentine and Scottsbluff, a killing freeze after May 1 was essentially a coin flip.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Last Spring Frost and Freeze Information
facts.quote: Falls City hasn't dropped below 28°F after this date since 1944 ... Chances of a killing freeze after May 1 go up to about four in 10 for North Platte and is essentially a coin-flip for Valentine and Scottsbluff.

facts.fact: Barge rates out of St. Louis usually hover around $20 a ton. During the low Mississippi River of October 2022, the spot rate hit a record $106.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Low Mississippi River Barge Disruptions (2022)
facts.quote: Historically barge rates have hovered around $20 per a ton. ... Louis barge spot rate hit a record $106 per ton during the week of Oct 11.
facts.note: 2022 is the year of the article (November 2022), which covers that fall.

facts.fact: Grain barges are usually loaded to an 11 to 12 foot draft in fall. Low water in 2022 forced 9-foot limits, cutting 10,000 to 15,000 bushels per barge.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Low Mississippi River Barge Disruptions (2022)
facts.quote: Typically, barges are loaded to a 11-12 foot draft during the fall, but companies started imposing 9-foot barge draft restrictions in October, which can lead to a reduction of 10,000-15,000 bushels per barge (Wicks, 2022).

facts.fact: Most US soybean exports leave through the Gulf, and 94% of those ride Mississippi River barges to Louisiana.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Low Mississippi River Barge Disruptions (2022)
facts.quote: The vast majority of U.S. soybean exports get shipped out through the Gulf port, 94% of which rely on the Mississippi River barge system to get to Louisiana (Munch, 2022).

facts.fact: A Mississippi River tow normally pushes 30 to 40 barges. Low water in 2022 cut tows to 25.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Low Mississippi River Barge Disruptions (2022)
facts.quote: The slowdown during this period coincides with river closures (McWhirter, 2022) and restrictions on barge companies that reduced the bar tow, normally 30-40 barges to 25 (Kennedy, 2022).

facts.fact: A 2025 farmdoc daily analysis found cereal grains were 58% of the farm and food freight moved by US rail and 52% on waterways, but only 35% on highways.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Agri-Food Transportation by Highway, Railway, and Waterway in the United States (2025)
facts.quote: Notably, cereal grains (SCTG 02) dominate flows on railways and waterways—accounting for 58% and 52% of mass moved on those modes, respectively—while they constitute a smaller fraction on highways (35%).

facts.fact: In Brazil, grain is trucked about 440 miles on average from farm to rail or barge. In the US the haul to an inland elevator is about 25 to 100 miles.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Investments in Brazilian Grain Transportation Shrink U.S. Logistical Advantage (2022)
facts.quote: In Brazil, short-haul trucking averages about 440 miles from farm to rail and barge terminals. In the United States, the average distance from farm to inland grain elevator terminals is about 25-100 miles (Salin, 2021).

facts.fact: From 2011 to 2020, Brazil's corn and soybean exports through its northern ports rose 410%, from 8.3 million to 42.3 million tons.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Investments in Brazilian Grain Transportation Shrink U.S. Logistical Advantage (2022)
facts.quote: Between 2011 and 2020, Brazilian exports of corn and soybeans through the northern and northeastern ports increased by 410%, from 8.3 million tons to 42.3 million tons

facts.fact: The 663-mile stretch of Brazil's BR-163 highway from Sorriso, Mato Grosso, to the northern state of Para was finished only in late November 2019.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Investments in Brazilian Grain Transportation Shrink U.S. Logistical Advantage (2022)
facts.quote: The 663-mile stretch of BR-163 from Sorriso, North Mato Grosso, to Pará was completed in late November 2019.

facts.fact: A 2024 report found H-2A guest workers made up 15% of employment on US crop farms, and farms in all states used the program.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Growing Role of H-2A Workers in U.S. Agriculture (2025)
facts.quote: H-2A workers now account for 15% of employment on U.S. crop farms (Castillo, Martin, and Rutledge, 2024). ... Farms in all states across the U.S. utilize the H-2A program.

facts.fact: The Southeast had almost 1.3 million farm jobs in 1969 and 612,000 in 2021. It went from 35 people per farm job to 140.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Changes in Farm Employment, 1969 to 2021 (2023)
facts.quote: The Southeast region had 612,000 farm jobs in 2021—down from almost 1.3 million in 1969. ... Consider that in 1969, the Southeast region had 35 people for every farm job; by 2021, there were 140 people per farm job.

facts.fact: A 2023 farmdoc daily article reports that in North and South Dakota, farm employment was 5.2% of total employment, more than in any other state.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Changes in Farm Employment, 1969 to 2021 (2023)
facts.quote: In North and South Dakota, farm employment represents 5.2% of total employment which is greater than in any other state.

facts.fact: Feedstock used for US renewable diesel grew from a little over 2 billion pounds in 2017 to over 22 billion in 2023, nearly eleven-fold.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, FAME Biodiesel, Renewable Diesel, and Biomass-Based Diesel Feedstock Trends over 2011-2023 (2024)
facts.quote: As recently as 2017 total feedstock usage for renewable diesel was a little over two billion pounds. This surged to over 22 billion pounds in 2023, a nearly eleven-fold increase.
facts.note: two billion is written as 2 billion.

facts.fact: Used cooking oil, called yellow grease, went from under 100 million pounds of US biofuel feedstock in 2015 to over 6 billion pounds in 2023.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, FAME Biodiesel, Renewable Diesel, and Biomass-Based Diesel Feedstock Trends over 2011-2023 (2024)
facts.quote: Yellow grease feedstock increased the most, from under 100 million pounds in 2015 to over 6 billion pounds in 2023.
facts.note: Yellow grease is the trade name for used cooking oil.

facts.fact: In 2022, the 2,013 US farms with 1,000 or more cows sold 66% of all the milk.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, US Dairy Herds and Policy and the 2022 Census of Agriculture (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, the 2,013 farms with 1,000 or more cows accounted for 66% of all US milk sales (see Figures 1 and 2).

facts.fact: The US made 226.4 billion pounds of milk in 2022, 5% more than in 2017, even though 39% fewer farms sold milk.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, US Dairy Herds and Policy and the 2022 Census of Agriculture (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, the US produced 226.4 billion pounds of milk, up from 215.5 billion pounds in 2017 or by 5% ... In total, 39% fewer US farms sold milk in 2022 than 2017.

facts.fact: Newer dairy states, mostly in the West, passed the traditional ones in milk output in 2004 and in cow numbers in 2020.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Production Trends in the US Dairy Sector (2023)
facts.quote: Rapid production growth in modern states led their output to exceed traditional states in 2004. ... in 2020 the number of cows in modern dairy states was higher than traditional dairy states for the first time.

facts.fact: Since 2010, milk per cow in traditional dairy states rose about 18%, against 8% in newer Western dairy states, about when genomic testing of bulls arrived.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Production Trends in the US Dairy Sector (2023)
facts.quote: While yield growth prior to 2010 was roughly the same in both regions, traditional states have increased milk yield about 18% since 2010, compared to just 8% growth in modern dairy states. This change in relative yield growth happens to coincide with an increase in the genetic milk yield potential of dairy bulls due to the introduction of genomic testing

facts.fact: Since 1980, harvested crop acres in the US South fell by 13.4 million, while cotton acres fell by 3.4 million.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Evolving US Southern Crop Problem (2026)
facts.quote: However, since 1980, or roughly the last 50 years, harvested acres of all crops in the US South have declined by 13.4 million, much greater than the 3.4 million decline in cotton harvested acres

facts.fact: July 2012 ran about six degrees above average in Illinois, Indiana and Iowa. Before 2012, the worst recent season for US corn and soybeans was 1988.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, How Bad Was the 2012 Corn and Soybean Growing Season? (2012)
facts.quote: Prior to 2012, the most adverse growing season weather conditions for U.S. corn and soybeans in recent history occurred in 1988. ... July was astonishingly hot in all three states in 2012, with temperatures about six degrees above average.

facts.fact: In the 2012 drought, Kentucky corn made just 47% of trend yield and Illinois 62%, 105 bushels against 169. South Carolina hit 131% of trend.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Locating the 2012 Drought Using State Corn Yields (2013)
facts.quote: This means that the 2012 yield of 105 bushels is 62% of the 169 bushel trend yield. ... Relative to trend yields, the lowest yields were in Kentucky (47% of trend) and Missouri (53%). ... States with exceptionally high yields include South Carolina (131% of trend)

facts.fact: From 1989 to 2023, Illinois crop insurance paid out 62 cents for each premium dollar, against 94 cents for the whole US. In 2022 it was just 10 cents.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Crop Insurance Loss Performance in Illinois and the Midwest (2024)
facts.quote: A loss ratio of 1.0 means that crop insurance payments equal the total premium. ... The Illinois loss ratio was .28 in 2020, .13 in 2021, and .10 in 2022. ... From 1989 to 2023, the loss ratio for Illinois averaged .62 compared to .94 for the U.S.
facts.note: Loss ratios .62, .94 and .10 are written as cents paid per premium dollar.

facts.fact: Nebraska corn produced 26 bushels an acre in the 1900s. In 2009 it set a record of 178.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: Corn production in terms of bushels/acre has increased dramatically over the years –from 26 bushels/acre produced in Nebraska in the 1900s to 178 bushels per acre (a new record) produced in 2009.

facts.fact: A corn plant averages about 8 feet tall by midsummer, and a healthy plant's roots can reach 6 1/2 feet into the ground.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: A corn plant can be anywhere from 5 to 12 feet tall, on average 8 ft tall by midsummer and a healthy corn's roots can reach 6 ½ feet into the ground!
facts.note: 6 ½ is written as 6 1/2.

facts.fact: Nebraska soybeans averaged 14 bushels an acre in the 1920s and more than 54 in 2009.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: Nebraska soybean yields in 2009 averaged more than 54 bushels per acre; in the 1920's average yield was 14 bushels/acre.

facts.fact: A soybean plant flowers in summer and makes 60 to 80 pods, each usually holding three beans.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: During the summer, soybeans flower and produce 60-80 pods, each holding three pea-sized beans.

facts.fact: About 30 thousand wheat varieties are sorted into just six market classes.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: Six classes bring order to about 30 thousand varieties of wheat.

facts.fact: A 60-pound bushel of wheat makes about 42 pounds of white flour, or 42 loaves of white bread at a pound and a half each.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop & Plant Science Facts
facts.quote: One bushel of wheat weighs approximately 60 pounds. One bushel of wheat yields approximately 42 pounds of white flour. ... A bushel of wheat yields 42 commercial loaves of white bread (one-and-a-half pound loaves).

facts.fact: Ohio's line fence law lets a landowner go up to 10 feet onto a neighbor's land to build or keep up a boundary fence, but they are liable for damage.
facts.source: Ohio State University Agricultural and Resource Law Program, Farm Office blog
facts.quote: Also, Ohio’s line fence law in ORC 971.08 allows you to access up to 10 feet of the neighbor’s property to build the fence, although you can be liable if you damage the property in doing so.

facts.fact: For Ohio's farm use property tax value, a parcel must be 10 acres or more in commercial farming, or gross $2,500 a year from it if smaller.
facts.source: Ohio State University Agricultural and Resource Law Program, Farm Office blog
facts.quote: The definition of a “farm” is the same as the CAUV eligibility—a parcel devoted to commercial agricultural production that is either 10 acres or more or, if under 10 acres, grosses $2500 annually from agricultural production.

facts.fact: Alfalfa digestibility falls from about 75% at bud stage to below 60% at full bloom.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Evaluating Alfalfa Stands Part II: Renovation Options (2020)
facts.quote: Following the same maturity stage, digestibility steadily decreases from 75% to below 60% when going from the bud stage to the full bloom stage, respectively.

facts.fact: Twenty years of USDA research in Nebraska put the nitrogen credit from a soybean crop to the next corn crop at about 55 pounds an acre dryland and 65 irrigated.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Giving Proper Nitrogen Credit for Legumes in Corn and Milo Rotations
facts.quote: The result of 20 years of research in Nebraska by USDA-ARS finds the mean soybean nitrogen credit to be about 55 lb/acre for dryland and 65 lb/acre for irrigated production.
facts.note: Twenty is written out at the start of the sentence for 20.

facts.fact: After calving, a beef cow's energy needs rise about 30% and her protein needs nearly double.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Pasture and Forage Minute: Understanding ADF and NDF, Hay Quality After Calving (2023)
facts.quote: Energy requirements increase about 30% and protein needs nearly double after calving.

facts.fact: Fiber in feed, measured as NDF, runs as high as 80% in straw and under 40% in early-bloom alfalfa.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Pasture and Forage Minute: Understanding ADF and NDF, Hay Quality After Calving (2023)
facts.quote: NDF levels can vary from 80% in straw to less than 40% in early blooming alfalfa.

facts.fact: A well pumping 450 gallons a minute puts down 1 acre-inch of water every hour.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, How Does Hot, Dry, Windy Weather Affect Corn Plants Now?
facts.quote: When figuring your well's capacity, a good conversion factor to remember is that 450 gallons per minute applies 1 acre-inch of water every hour.

facts.fact: Drought-stressed corn at the 6 to 8 leaf stage may set ears of 12 to 14 rows, where the same hybrid with good moisture sets 16 to 20.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, How Does Hot, Dry, Windy Weather Affect Corn Plants Now?
facts.quote: (This usually occurs at about the 6- to 8-leaf stage). ... These stressed plants will likely produce ears with 12-14 rows, while the same hybrid with better moisture will produce 16-20 rows—a yield constraint by the time it is knee high.

facts.fact: Through the 5-leaf stage, a corn plant's growing point is still below ground. A plant that loses five leaves then can still reach 19 to 21 leaves at tassel.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Assessing Early-season Hail Damage on Corn
facts.quote: Up through the 5-leaf stage of growth, the growing point of corn is below the soil surface. ... If the plant loses five of those leaves early on, it will still have the potential to have 19 to 21 leaves at tasseling.

facts.fact: Corn sets its ear row number by the 12-leaf stage, but kernels per row are not set until about V17, just before tassel.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Assessing Early-season Hail Damage on Corn
facts.quote: The number of rows that will be in the ear is established by the 12-leaf stage. ... The number of kernels per row is not determined until about V17, just before tasseling.

facts.fact: Before hybrid corn spread in the 1930s, US farmers planted over 100 million acres of corn. A 2025 farmdoc daily article puts the average since 2007 at about 91 million.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Fringe Acres and US Average Corn Yield (2025)
facts.quote: Prior to the adoption of hybrid corn beginning in the 1930s, the US planted over 100 million acres of corn. ... Since 2007, corn acres have trended up slightly around an average level of about 91 million acres.

facts.fact: Extra corn acres do not drag down the national yield much: how far acres stray from normal explains only about 3% of yield swings from trend.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Fringe Acres and US Average Corn Yield (2025)
facts.quote: Acreage deviations explain only about 3 percent of observed year-to-year variation in yield deviations from trend.

facts.fact: From 1995-1997 to 2024-2026, US barley acres fell 65%, from 7 million to 2 million. Oats fell 56%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Yield Increases of Grains and Major Crops in the United States (2026)
facts.quote: A summary of acreage changes from 1995-1997 to 2024-2026 is: ... Barley acres decreased from 7 million to 2 million, a decrease of 65%. ... Oat acres decreased from 5 million to 2 million, a decrease of 56%.

facts.fact: US wheat acres dropped from 71 million in 1995-1997 to 45 million in 2024-2026, while soybeans grew from 66 million to 84 million.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Yield Increases of Grains and Major Crops in the United States (2026)
facts.quote: A summary of acreage changes from 1995-1997 to 2024-2026 is: ... Soybean acres increased from 66 million to 84 million, an increase of 29%. Wheat acres decreased from 71 million to 45 million, a decrease of 37%.

facts.fact: US food inflation hit 11.4% in August 2022, the biggest yearly rise since May 1979.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Inflation and Food Price Update: May 2025
facts.quote: In August 2022, the rate of inflation for food reached 11.4%, the largest annual increase since May 1979.

facts.fact: From December 2019 to April 2025, restaurant and other food away from home rose 31.9% in price, against 28.2% for groceries.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Inflation and Food Price Update: May 2025
facts.quote: Since December 2019, prices for food away from home have risen 31.9% compared to 28.2% for food at home. In April, prices for food away from home rose 0.4% from last month
facts.note: April 2025 is the month of the CPI data the article reports (May 2025 update).

facts.fact: The 2014-2015 bird flu outbreak hit 45 million US birds by June 2015. Iowa alone culled 29.2 million.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Economic Implications of the 2014-2015 Bird Flu (2015)
facts.quote: The total number of U.S. birds affected stands at 45 million, and includes 37.5 million chickens and 7.4 million turkeys. ... States hit hardest by the bird flu include Iowa with 29.2 million birds culled and Minnesota with 8.4 million birds culled.
facts.note: June 2015 is the article's date.

facts.fact: Excellent Illinois farmland rose from $10,695 an acre in 2020 to $16,779 in 2023, up 57%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Prices and Government Programs (2026)
facts.quote: It increased from $10,695 per acre in 2020 to $16,779 in 2023, an increase of $6,084 per acre, or 57%.

facts.fact: In 1985, Illinois cash rent averaged 8.0% of land value, when 10-year Treasury notes paid 10.62%. By 2015 notes paid 2.14%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Cash Rent as a Percent of Farmland Price (2016)
facts.quote: For state-level averages in Illinois, cash rent as a percent of land value averaged 8.0% in 1985. ... Ten-year notes averaged a 10.62% yield in 1985, falling to 2.14% in 2015.
facts.note: Ten-year is written as 10-year.

facts.fact: No crop reached 100% of parity even in the ethanol price era. The closest was wheat, at 84% of parity in March 2008.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Considering Policy Reversion: The Parity Paradox (2019)
facts.quote: No commodity reached 100% of parity during the entire RFS-influenced price era. The highest was wheat at 84% of parity in March 2008.

facts.fact: As of 2019, USDA's NASS still figured parity prices against a base of 1910-1914. As calculated then, no commodity was above 40% of parity.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Considering Policy Reversion: The Parity Paradox (2019)
facts.quote: NASS continues to calculate parity prices, using the monthly prices received and converted to the indexes for the parity base period (1910-1914 = 100) to compute the parity prices and ratios ... It is notable that, as currently calculated, not a single commodity is above 40% of the parity price.

facts.fact: US cotton yields were 213 pounds an acre in 1933 and 517 by 1963. Wheat went from 11 or 12 bushels to 25.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Considering Policy Reversion: The Parity Paradox (2019)
facts.quote: For example, wheat yields were around 11 or 12 bushels per acre when the parity system was created. By the time wheat farmers rejected supply controls in the 1963 wheat referendum, wheat yields were 25 bushels per acre (179% of the 1926-1933 average). Similarly, cotton yields were 213 pounds per acre in 1933 but had increased to 517 pounds per acre by 1963

facts.fact: In the 1963 wheat referendum, wheat farmers voted down federal supply controls.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Considering Policy Reversion: The Parity Paradox (2019)
facts.quote: By the time wheat farmers rejected supply controls in the 1963 wheat referendum

facts.fact: US trend corn yields drifted slightly down through 1936, then rose. The fastest gain was 2.6 bushels an acre a year, from 1956 to 1969.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Role of Weather in the Pattern of Corn Prices over Time (2017)
facts.quote: Trend corn yields through 1936 actually had a small tendency to decline, but have risen ever since. The highest annual rate of growth in trend yields, 2.6 bushels per acre, occurred during 1956-1969.

facts.fact: USDA did not fully adopt modern random sampling to estimate crop yields until the 1960s.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Role of Weather in the Pattern of Corn Prices over Time (2017)
facts.quote: Modern random sampling methods to estimate yields were not fully adopted by the USDA until the 1960s.

facts.fact: In US corn records back to 1895, the worst 20-year run of weather for yields was 1917 to 1936. The best was 1937 to 1956.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Role of Weather in the Pattern of Corn Prices over Time (2017)
facts.quote: The sums of the deviations vary considerably by time period, with the largest cumulative negative deviation occurring in the 20-year period from 1917 to 1936 and the largest cumulative positive deviation occurring in the 20-year window from 1937 to 1956. ... The first window is 1895 through 1914

facts.fact: Nebraska's Knorr-Holden plot has been farmed since 1912. After 71 years of manure, its soil held about 16% more plant-available water and twice the organic carbon.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Soil Amendments (2020)
facts.quote: The Knorr-Holden Plot was started in 1912 and the annual treatment of cattle manure at 27 Mg ha-1 was introduced in 1942. ... Manured plots also retained about 16% more plant available water compared with non-manured plots and had twice as much soil organic carbon concentration ... Overall, 71 years of manure application reduced compactibility and increased water retention in this semiarid soil.

facts.fact: Brothers Jim and Clifford Barta gave their 6,000-acre Sandhills ranch near Rose to the University of Nebraska in 1996 for research.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, UNL Study: Nebraska's Sandhills Dunes May Be More Stable Than Thought
facts.quote: Wedin's experiments are being conducted on about 30 acres of the former Barta Brothers Ranch near Rose, a 6,000-acre Sandhills ranch donated to UNL in 1996 by brothers Jim and Clifford Barta.

facts.fact: From 1980 to 2015, US corn yields rose 61% while soil erosion per unit of corn fell 58%. For soybeans it was 29% and 47%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop Residue and High-Carbon Char: Potential Soil Conservation Tools (2018)
facts.quote: Between 1980 and 2015, corn and soybean yields in the U.S. improved by 61% and 29%, respectively, with corresponding decline in soil erosion by 58% and 47%.
facts.note: "Per unit of corn": the page's chart is an index of resource use to produce corn and soybean.

facts.fact: Covering 30% of the ground with residue cuts wind erosion about 70%. At 60% cover, the cut is about 90%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop Residue and High-Carbon Char: Potential Soil Conservation Tools (2018)
facts.quote: Ground covers of 30% and 60% are estimated to reduce wind erosion by 70% and 90% percent, respectively

facts.fact: Keeping soil organic matter steady takes an estimated 2 to 3 tons of crop residue an acre each year. Two tons of corn residue usually covers about 50% of the ground.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop Residue and High-Carbon Char: Potential Soil Conservation Tools (2018)
facts.quote: Our best estimate of the minimum amount of residue that is needed to maintain soil organic matter is 2 or 3 ton/acre/year. (Two tons of corn residue usually gives about 50% cover.)

facts.fact: A seed soaks up most of its water in the first 24 hours after planting, the time soil must stay near 50°F. After that, seedlings tolerate soil as cold as 35 to 40°F.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Early Planting: Using Soil Temperature Windows for Corn and Soybean
facts.quote: corn and soybean are safe to plant at 50°F or greater soil temperature ... Soil temperature above the thresholds during the first 24 hours after planting is critical for adequate water uptake (imbibition phase) to ensure good germination. ... During the osmotic phase, water uptake slows, and seedlings in this phase are quite tolerant of soil temperatures as low as 35-40°F.

facts.fact: In Nebraska, an eight-day earlier date for half the irrigated soybeans planted has gone with about 4 more bushels an acre. Earlier corn planting showed little such gain.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Early Planting: Using Soil Temperature Windows for Corn and Soybean
facts.quote: An eight-day advance in the Nebraska irrigated soybean 50% planting progress date was associated with a historic 4 bu/ac increase in irrigated soybean fields and a 2 bu/ac increase in rainfed fields. Delays in the Nebraska irrigated corn 50% planting progress date did not have much impact on corn yields.

facts.fact: Across studies, each extra gram of soil organic carbon raised water the soil can supply to plants by 1 to 4.9 grams per 100 grams of soil.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, The Water-Soil Health Connection (2017)
facts.quote: A review of several studies conducted across a range of soil textures reported that a 1 gram increase in soil organic carbon increased available water by 1 to 4.9 grams for every 100 grams of soil.

facts.fact: A review of 69 US studies found cover crops cut nitrate leaching by an average of 70%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, The Water-Soil Health Connection (2017)
facts.quote: Indeed,a meta-analysis of 69 separate studies from across the U.S. showed that cover crops reduced nitrate leaching losses by an average of 70%.

facts.fact: After six years of removing about 60% of corn residue in south central Nebraska, plant-available water fell from 1.61 to 1.21 inches per 4 inches of soil.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Cover Crop and Crop Residue Management: How Does it Affect Soil Water? (2018)
facts.quote: Additionally, after removing approximately 60% of the corn residue for six years, plant available water decreased from 1.61 inches to 1.21 inches per 4 inches of soil in south central Nebraska.

facts.fact: Building soil organic carbon enough to raise plant-available water takes more than 10 years. Long cover crop trials in Kansas, Maryland and Iowa needed 12.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Cover Crop and Crop Residue Management: How Does it Affect Soil Water? (2018)
facts.quote: Long-term, 12-year experiments in Kansas and Maryland have found that cover crops do increase water infiltration. Cover crops were found to increase plant available water after 12 years in an experiment in Iowa using cereal rye ... However, it takes time (more than 10 years) to increase soil organic carbon in the soil and improve the soil structure to increase plant available water.

facts.fact: The ear leaf and the leaves above it supply about 70% of a corn plant's yield, which is why leaf disease reaching the ear leaf early matters.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Gray Leaf Spot Severity Increasing Rapidly (2009)
facts.quote: Since the ear leaf and those above it contribute the most to yield (approximately 70%), it is especially concerning that the disease has already progressed to them this early in the season.
facts.note: approximately 70% is written as about 70%.

facts.fact: Gray leaf spot spores infect corn after 12 or more hours of wet leaves or canopy humidity over 90%, best at 70 to 90°F. Lesions take 14 to 28 days to show.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Gray Leaf Spot Severity Increasing Rapidly (2009)
facts.quote: If rain or irrigation water is available or there is high canopy humidity (>90%) for at least 12 hours, these spores may germinate and infect the plant. The optimal temperature range for infection is 70-90°F ... After infection, lesion development and further spore production on the leaf takes 14-28 days, depending on conditions and hybrid resistance.

facts.fact: In southwest Nebraska, yields of corn hybrids susceptible and resistant to Goss's wilt have differed by as much as 65 bushels an acre.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Goss's Wilt in Corn (2009)
facts.quote: Differences in yield between susceptible and resistant hybrids with the leaf blight phase of the disease have reportedly been as high as 65 bushels per acre in southwest Nebraska in recent years.

facts.fact: Southern rust of corn was confirmed in 45 Nebraska counties in 2020. It thrives near 80°F in moist weather.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Crop Diseases Spreading and Increasing (2020)
facts.quote: Southern rust has been confirmed in 45 Nebraska counties. ... Warm temperatures, especially around 80 F and moist conditions favor southern rust development and spread.
facts.note: 2020 is the year of the article.

facts.fact: Sudden death syndrome of soybeans was first seen in Nebraska in 2004, in Nemaha and Pierce counties.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, ILeVO Seed Treatment Shows Promise for Sudden Death Syndrome (2016)
facts.quote: Sudden death syndrome was first observed in Nebraska in 2004 in Nemaha and Pierce counties in eastern Nebraska.

facts.fact: By 2016, soybean cyst nematode had been found in 58 Nebraska counties that grow 93% of the state's soybeans.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Test for SCN This Fall & Select Seed Accordingly (2016)
facts.quote: SCN has been identified in 58 Nebraska counties which produce 93% of the state's soybeans.
facts.note: 2016 is the year of the article.

facts.fact: Of more than 7,600 Nebraska soil samples tested for soybean cyst nematode from 2005 to 2016, over 30% came back positive.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Test for SCN This Fall & Select Seed Accordingly (2016)
facts.quote: Since 2005, more than 7,600 soil samples have been processed through this program for SCN and over 30% of them came back positive.

facts.fact: US tractor prices rose 14% over the nine years from 2011 to 2020, then 21% in just three years from 2020 to 2023.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Large Increase in Machinery Costs Suggests Need to Reconsider Machinery Purchase Decisions (2025)
facts.quote: The index increased to 114 in 2020, representing a 14% rise over the nine years from 2011 to 2020. ... From 2020 to 2023, tractor prices increased by 21%

facts.fact: A 2025 farmdoc daily analysis gives at least 3,000 acres as a benchmark for economical combine operation.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Large Increase in Machinery Costs Suggests Need to Reconsider Machinery Purchase Decisions (2025)
facts.quote: A benchmark for economical combine operation is at least 3,000 acres, with additional cost savings possible for farms harvesting above 3,000 acres.

facts.fact: In warm, breezy fall weather, standing corn can lose as much as 1% grain moisture a day. The target at harvest is 15%, and 13% for soybeans.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Cost Management: Harvest Operations (2020)
facts.quote: For corn, once the crop has reached maturity the desirable moisture level for grain at harvest is 15%. Elevated autumn temperatures can lead to rapid grain moisture loss, with losses as great as 1% per day when temperatures are high and particularly when also breezy ... The desirable moisture level for harvested soybeans is 13% moisture.

facts.fact: Yield monitors have been around since the mid-1990s. A 2019 report found over 68% of US farmers had one, but only 45% of the area was yield mapped.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Top Five Digital Agriculture Technologies Used in Nebraska
facts.quote: Yield monitors and yield maps have been around since the mid-1990s. ... It was reported that many farmers in the U.S. have a yield monitor (+68%), but only 45% of the area was yield mapped (Lowenberg-DeBoer and Erickson, 2019).

facts.fact: 41% of Nebraska farms used precision ag practices in 2025, down from 55% in 2023. 85% used smartphones.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Technology Use on Nebraska Farms in 2025
facts.quote: Other forms of technology used on Nebraska farms includes smartphones, 85%, and tablets, 39%. ... Forty-one percent of Nebraska farms were using precision ag practices to manage crops or livestock in 2025, compared to 55% in 2023.
facts.note: Forty-one percent is written as 41%.

facts.fact: 87% of Nebraska farms had internet in 2025. 74% got it by cell signal and 28% by satellite; 5% still used dial-up.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Technology Use on Nebraska Farms in 2025
facts.quote: In Nebraska, 87% of farms in Nebraska had internet access, down 3% from 2023. Methods used in Nebraska to access the internet included: cellular, 74%; broadband, 54%; satellite, 28%; dialup, 5%; other, 1%.
facts.note: 2025 is the year of the USDA survey named in the page title.

facts.fact: The 2023 US calf crop, 33.6 million head, was the smallest since 1940.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Records are Made to be Broken! (2024)
facts.quote: The calf crop at 33.6 million head or 2% below the prior year is, as expected, the lowest since 1940
facts.note: The report is USDA's January 1, 2024 inventory, so the calf crop is the 2023 crop.

facts.fact: Of the 13.8 million US cattle on feed on January 1, 2026, about 82.7% were in feedlots with capacity over 1,000 head.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Extending the Cattle Cycle with Still Lower Inventories (2026)
facts.quote: The inventory report puts cattle on feed at 13.8 million head as of January 1 ... About 82.7% of those animals or over 11.5 million head are in feedlots with capacity exceeding 1,000 head
