facts.fact: The January 1, 2026 USDA cattle report put the US herd in a seventh consecutive year of contraction, with fewer beef cows than at any time since 1960.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Extending the Cattle Cycle with Still Lower Inventories (2026)
facts.quote: The USDA’s cattle inventory report places the total number of cattle and calves on January 1 ... as the industry continues into a seventh consecutive year of contraction within the cattle cycle. ... Like last year, the report again confirms anticipated year over year drops across most inventory categories with fewer beef cows than any time since 1960
facts.note: 2026 is the year of the report (February 2026 article). The page's total head count is left out.

facts.fact: A 2024 farmdoc daily article says roughly 60% of the corn and soybeans produced in Illinois remain to be sold at the end of the calendar year.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Post-harvest Grain Marketing: Do Farmers Reap the Benefits? (2024)
facts.quote: Roughly 60% of corn and soybeans produced in Illinois remain to be sold at the end of the calendar year, but this aggregate number hides much variation across farmers.

facts.fact: Since 1973, the average US cash corn price has peaked in June at 113% of the October harvest low.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Net Return to Storing US Corn and Soybeans Since 1973 (2025)
facts.quote: Although US cash corn price since 1973 has averaged nearly the same in October ($2.992) and November ($2.993), October is used as the harvest low price month. ... (corn’s peak was 113% in June).

facts.fact: Since 1973, the US cash corn price in July beat June in only 39% of years. September beat June in 32%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Net Return to Storing US Corn and Soybeans Since 1973 (2025)
facts.quote: Although US cash corn price since 1973 has averaged nearly the same in October ($2.992) and November ($2.993) ... US cash price was higher in roughly one-third of the years after June, specifically, 39%, 32%, and 32% of the years for July, August, and September, respectively.

facts.fact: Illinois corn averaged $2.42 a bushel from 1973 to 2006. In the ethanol era that followed, it averaged $4.57 through April 2017.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Are There Predictable Crop Price Cycles? (2017)
facts.quote: the second era encompassed 1973 through November 2006 ... The average price of corn in the era was $2.42 per bushel. ... Through April 2017, the monthly average price of corn in Illinois in the current era is $4.57 per bushel

facts.fact: The early freeze of 1974 and the droughts of 1983, 1988 and 1995 each sent corn prices jumping for long stretches before they fell back.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Are There Predictable Crop Price Cycles? (2017)
facts.quote: The early freeze of 1974 and the drought years 1983, 1988, and 1995, in particular, are reflected in price jumps during the era and are associated with extended periods of above average prices that eventually return to the mean.

facts.fact: In FY2022 the average SNAP benefit was just over $230 a person a month, less than $8 a day or about $2.50 a meal, for 41.2 million people.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, A View of the Farm Bill Through Policy Design, Part 3: SNAP (2023)
facts.quote: to provide assistance to a monthly average of 41.2 million Americans ... USDA FNS reported that the average benefit per participating person each month was just over $230 in FY 2022—that would amount to less than $8 per day, or about $2.50 per meal.

facts.fact: A household's SNAP benefit is the maximum minus 30 percent of net income, so it drops 30 cents for each extra dollar earned. More than 30% of SNAP households have earnings.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Farm Bill Stalemate, Part 2: The SNAP Question (2018)
facts.quote: More than 30% of all SNAP households had earned income and are considered “working poor” (Oliveira et al., 2018). ... In general, a household’s SNAP benefit is equal to the maximum available ($649 for a household of four in FY2016) minus 30 percent of net income, meaning that benefits are reduced $0.30 for every $1.00 of net income.
facts.note: $0.30 is written as 30 cents.

facts.fact: Bacon and breakfast sausage normally come from only about 18% of a hog's carcass weight.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, What Happens When Food Marketers Require Restrictive Farming Practices? (2015)
facts.quote: may require only that portion of the hog used to produce bacon and breakfast sausage–normally about 18% of the carcass weight of a hog.

facts.fact: Plant-based meat made up an estimated 1.4% of total US meat sales around 2020.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Overview of the Meatless Meat Industry (2021)
facts.quote: The Good Food Institute estimates that meatless meat sales comprise 1.4% of total meat sales in the U.S.
facts.note: Around 2020: the article is from July 2021 and cites estimates from 2019 to 2021.

facts.fact: Singapore was the first country to approve the commercial sale of lab-grown meat, a chicken product, as reported in 2021.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Overview of the Meatless Meat Industry (2021)
facts.quote: Singapore is the first country to certify commercial sale of the product, with a lab-grown chicken product made by the American company Eat Just (Gilchrist 2021).

facts.fact: Studies put the share of consumers who would swap meat for a plant-based version at 25 to 30%, if both cost the same.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Consumer Preferences and the Meatless Meat Industry (2021)
facts.quote: Current studies indicate that 25-30% of consumers would be willing to substitute meatless meat for animal meat if both products were priced the same.

facts.fact: On Illinois grain farms, 2006 was the last year more land was crop-shared than cash-rented. By 2023, 48 percent was cash-rented and 27 percent crop-shared.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Tenure Characteristics of Illinois Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: From 2019 to 2023, the amount of land crop shared decreased from 32 percent to 27 percent while the amount of land cash rented increased from 45 percent to 48 percent. ... The last year where a larger amount of the farmland was crop shared compared to cash rented was in 2006.

facts.fact: Illinois grain farmers owned only 24 percent of the land they farmed in 2023. In central Illinois it was 15 percent.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Tenure Characteristics of Illinois Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: Southern Illinois farm operators own 27 percent of their land while central Illinois operators own only 15 percent. ... On a statewide basis, operators owned 24 percent of their land in 2023.

facts.fact: In 2023, northern Illinois farmers cash-rented 66 percent of their land, while central Illinois farmers crop-shared 37 percent.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Tenure Characteristics of Illinois Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: For example, in 2023, farmers in northern Illinois cash rented 66 percent of their land and crop shared 16 percent while central Illinois farmers cash rented 48 percent and crop shared 37 percent.

facts.fact: From 2000 to 2021, Illinois share rents averaged $229 an acre, just $9 more than cash rents. Share rent ran higher in the boom years 2003 to 2012.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Variable Cash Rental Arrangements in 2023
facts.quote: From 2000 to 2021, share rents averaged $229 per acre, $9 per acre higher than the average cash rent. ... Share rent levels were above cash rents from 2003 to 2012, when operator and land returns were high.

facts.fact: Of 584 new futures contracts launched worldwide in 2011, 52% never traded even once.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, How Many Futures Contracts Can One Market Support? (2012)
facts.quote: A recent report by Futures and Options World found that of the 584 new contracts launched worldwide in 2011, 52% failed to trade even one time.

facts.fact: In 2012, a new rival exchange offered grain futures nearly around the clock, and the CBOT answered by going to 22 hours of trading a day.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, How Many Futures Contracts Can One Market Support? (2012)
facts.quote: Trading hours will be from 8 PM Sunday to 6 PM Friday, which is substantially longer than the CBOT’s current 6:00 PM to 7:15 AM and 9:30 AM to 1:15 PM trading day. ... In this particular case, the CBOT announced that it would increase its trading hours to 22 hours a day, beginning later this month, to match the ICE trading hours.
facts.note: 2012 is the year of the article (May 2012).

facts.fact: In 1973 the Soviet Union made large grain purchases, reversing a trade policy dating to the Bolshevik Revolution. From 1973 to 2005, corn prices averaged $2.36 a bushel.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Are Long-Run Prices Still $4 for Corn, $10 for Soybeans, and $5.50 for Wheat? (2022)
facts.quote: In 1973, the Soviet Union made large grain purchases, reversing trade policy dating back to the Bolshevik Revolution, thereby open more markets to global trade. From 1973 to 2005, corn prices averaged $2.36 per bushel.

facts.fact: US corn averaged $3.24 a bushel in 1995 and fell to $1.94 in 1998.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Are Long-Run Prices Still $4 for Corn, $10 for Soybeans, and $5.50 for Wheat? (2022)
facts.quote: Sometimes corn prices were considerably above the $2.36 average, as occurred in 1995 when corn prices were $3.24 per bushel. ... Corn prices again went below the $2.36 average, falling to $1.94 per bushel in 1998.

facts.fact: Only 4 Bt proteins target corn rootworm. In many Nebraska counties, rootworms beat single-trait hybrids planted more than three years in a row.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Corn Rootworm Management Update (2018)
facts.quote: Four types of Bt proteins target corn rootworms: Cry3Bb1, mCry3A, eCry3.1Ab, and Cry34/35Ab1. In multiple counties across Nebraska, greater than expected injury has been observed or resistance confirmed when single trait Cry3Bb1 or mCry3A hybrids have been planted for more than three consecutive years.
facts.note: Four is written as 4.

facts.fact: Bt corn aimed at European corn borer has been widely available since the late 1990s, and as of 2019 the Bt proteins in use killed over 99.9% of borer larvae.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, First ECB Resistance to Bt Corn Reported in Canada (2019)
facts.quote: Widely available since the late 1990s, Bt corn hybrids targeting ECB are grown throughout the U.S. ... Current Bt proteins (i.e, Cry1Ab, Cry1A.105, Cry1F and Cry2Ab2) kill over 99.9% of the ECB larvae

facts.fact: The first field resistance of European corn borer to a Bt corn protein, Cry1F, was confirmed in Nova Scotia, Canada, in 2019.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, First ECB Resistance to Bt Corn Reported in Canada (2019)
facts.quote: confirmed the resistance of ECB to the Cry1F protein in Bt corn hybrids in Nova Scotia, Canada.
facts.note: 2019 is the year of the article, titled First ECB Resistance to Bt Corn Reported in Canada.

facts.fact: US sows set a record of 11.92 pigs per litter in fall 2024. Denmark already averages around 15.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Record Pig Crop driven by Record Pigs per Litter (2024)
facts.quote: a 0.2% cut in sows farrowed was more than offset by 11.92 pigs per litter, up 2.3% from last year’s record for the period ... further productivity growth is feasible, as Denmark is recently averaging around 15 pigs per litter.
facts.note: Fall 2024 is the September-November quarter of the December 2024 report named on the page.

facts.fact: Americans ate an estimated 50.5 pounds of pork per person in 2024, still below the 52.1 pounds of 2019.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Record Pig Crop driven by Record Pigs per Litter (2024)
facts.quote: The USDA estimates U.S. per capita pork consumption at 50.5 pounds per person for 2024, and forecasts the number rising to 50.9 pounds per person in 2025, still below the pre-COVID-19 level of 52.1 pounds per person in 2019.

facts.fact: From 1994 to 2023, the US pig crop grew from 101.5 million to 135.8 million head while the sow herd grew only 0.17 percent a year.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Long-Term Trends in Pigs per Litter (2024)
facts.quote: The annual growth rate in the U.S. sow herd during the 1994 to 2023 period is only 0.17 percent per year. ... In 1994, the pig crop (swine production) was 101.5 million head (24.4 billion pounds). The pig crop in 2023 was 135.8 million head

facts.fact: Farm mortgage rates peaked at nearly 17.5% in the 1980s, and some loans then ran up to 40 years.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farmland Markets: Comparing the 1980s and the Present (2014)
facts.quote: In the 1980s, farm mortgage rates peaked at nearly 17.5% ... In addition, typical mortgage loans in the 1980s included longer amortization periods (up to 40 years in some cases) and higher loan-to-value fractions than is typical today.

facts.fact: US farm assets fell 22% from 1980 to 1988, to $789 billion. They did not pass the 1980 high again until 1996.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Agricultural Assets Compared to Agricultural Debt (2022)
facts.quote: From 1980 through 1988, agricultural assets were decreasing due to lower values of machinery and land due the farm crisis in the 1980s. ... By 1988, agricultural assets had declined by 22% reaching a level of $789 billion. ... At the end of 1996, agricultural assets reached $1,003 billion, surpassing the previous high set in 1980.

facts.fact: US farm debt passed gross farm income in 1977 and stayed above it through 1985. By then nearly a quarter of farm debt could not be repaid from income.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Other Side of the Seventies (2019)
facts.quote: As income began to fall after the spike, debt continued increasing at a steep pace, debt bypassing income in 1977. ... Debt remained above gross farm income through 1985. ... By 1985, estimates were that nearly a quarter of the farm debt could not be repaid from income (Bullock, 1985).

facts.fact: US farm exports jumped in 1972 and 1973 and kept rising through the 1970s, peaking in 1981.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Other Side of the Seventies (2019)
facts.quote: The change in exports beginning in 1972 and 1973 stand out compared to the years preceding them (average from 1960 to 1971 in gray area), but also that exports continued to increase throughout the 1970s, peaking in 1981.

facts.fact: Ten-year Treasury yields topped 15% in 1981, then trended down to a low of 1.37% on July 5, 2016.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Rising Interest Rates and Farmland Prices (2016)
facts.quote: Ten-year Treasury yields reached highs of over 15% in 1981. Since the 1981 highs, Treasury yields have been on a general downward trend, reaching a low of 1.37% on July 5, 2016.

facts.fact: Brazil's second corn crop is called safrinha, "little harvest" in Portuguese. As of 2022 it was the largest crop, about 70% of Brazil's corn.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Comparing Brazilian (1st and 2nd Crops), American, and Argentine Corn Yields (2022)
facts.quote: Initially smaller than the 1st crop, it was named the safrinha, “little harvest” in Portuguese. However, it is now the largest crop, accounting for 70% of Brazilian corn.

facts.fact: Brazil's share of world corn trade grew from 7.5% in 2010/11 to 22% in 2020/21.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Comparing Brazilian (1st and 2nd Crops), American, and Argentine Corn Yields (2022)
facts.quote: Brazil’s share of world corn trade increased from 7.5% percent in 2010/11 to 22% percent in 2020/21.

facts.fact: Before the 2022-23 season, Brazil had out-exported the US in corn only once, in the US drought year of 2012/13.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Will Brazil Emerge as the Number One Corn Exporting Nation? (2023)
facts.quote: Brazil exported more corn than the U.S. only once before, in the drought year of 2012/13. ... In its March “World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates (WASDE)” report, the USDA raised its forecast for Brazilian corn exports to 50 million tons for the 2022-23 marketing year

facts.fact: The first shipment of Brazilian corn to China sailed in November 2022. By January 2023 China was Brazil's top corn buyer.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Will Brazil Emerge as the Number One Corn Exporting Nation? (2023)
facts.quote: the first shipment of Brazilian corn to China occurred in November 2022. ... In January 2023, China became the primary destination of Brazilian corn exports by volume

facts.fact: Three La Nina winters in a row has happened only twice since 1950. The 1999-2001 run left US corn yields right on trend.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, What to Expect as Corn Yields Face a Third Straight La Nina (2022)
facts.quote: A triple La Niña has happened only twice since 1950. The last time La Nina was in place for three years in a row was from 1999 to 2001. ... And the last time that three consecutive La Niña happened (1999-2000-2001), the yields were just on the trendline.

facts.fact: Two of the worst US corn yields in recent decades, 1993 and 2012, came in ENSO-neutral years, not El Nino or La Nina years.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, What to Expect as Corn Yields Face a Third Straight La Nina (2022)
facts.quote: Also, two very low yield levels happened in Neutral years (1993 and 2012), and only one in a La Niña year (1995).

facts.fact: In Illinois and Iowa from 1960 on, going from the driest to the wettest winter changed corn yield by at most 5 bushels an acre.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Winter Precipitation and Corn Yield (2012)
facts.quote: Once again, the analysis is conducted for Illinois and Iowa (the two largest corn producing states) over the period 1960 through 2011. ... The yield impact of moving from the minimum to the maximum winter precipitation observed over 1960-2012 in both states is at most 5 bushels per acre.

facts.fact: An official bushel is 1.244 cubic feet. US No. 1 yellow corn must weigh at least 56 pounds per bushel.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Why Grain Test Weights Matter (2017)
facts.quote: Grain test weight, often used as a grain quality indicator, is a volumetric measurement based on an official bushel being 1.244 cubic feet. ... No. 1 yellow corn, the official minimum test weight is 56 pounds per bushel.

facts.fact: Corn kept below 50°F can be stored at 15% moisture. If it will be warmer, the safe level is about 13.5%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Maintaining Grain Quality During Long-Term Storage (2016)
facts.quote: If you can keep stored corn below 50 degrees, you can store it at 15% moisture. But if the temperature will be warmer, then the recommended storage moisture content is about 13.5%.

facts.fact: Stored grain insects go dormant below about 50°F and die if the grain stays below 30°F for a few weeks.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Maintaining Grain Quality During Long-Term Storage (2016)
facts.quote: "Insect reproduction is reduced below about 70 degrees, insects are dormant below about 50°F, and insects are killed if grain is below 30°F for a few weeks."

facts.fact: Allowable storage time for grain roughly doubles with each 10-degree drop in grain temperature.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Drying and Storage Tips (2016)
facts.quote: In addition, grain moisture content and temperature affect the rate of mold growth and grain deterioration, with the allowable storage time approximately doubling with each 10-degree reduction in grain temperature.

facts.fact: A 1-inch rain on an open corn pile raises the moisture of the top foot of grain by 9 percentage points.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Drying and Storage Tips (2016)
facts.quote: Just a 1-inch rain will increase the moisture content of a 1-foot layer of corn by 9 percentage points.

facts.fact: Losing just the top foot of a 25-foot-high cone-shaped grain pile loses about 13% of the grain.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Grain Drying and Storage Tips (2016)
facts.quote: A 1-foot loss on the surface of a 25-foot-high cone-shaped pile is about 13% of the grain.

facts.fact: Selling soybeans at 8% moisture instead of the 13% standard gives away about 5.43% of the crop's weight. At 12% it is 1.14%.
facts.source: University of Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch, Plan Harvest to Deliver Soybean at Optimum Moisture (2017)
facts.quote: Soybean delivered below or above 13% moisture — the elevator standard — lose potential profit. ... If you sell soybean at 8% moisture, you're losing about 5.43% of your yield; at 9% moisture, it's 4.4%; at 10% moisture, 3.3%; at 11% moisture, 2.25%; and at 12% moisture, it's 1.14% yield loss.

facts.fact: Illinois farmland prices more than doubled from 2003 to 2011, growing 9.2 percent a year compounded.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, A Historical Perspective on Illinois Farmland Sales (2013)
facts.quote: From 2003 to 2011, Illinois farmland prices more than doubled, reflecting 9.2 percent annually compounded growth.

facts.fact: In the 2012 drought, beef cow numbers fell 9 percent in the Southern Plains, while the wetter Northern Plains gained about 170,000 cows.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Where Have All the Beef Cows Gone? (2013)
facts.quote: The impacts were largest for producers in the Southern Plains where beef cow numbers dropped by 9 percent last year ... Likely some of those cows moved to the Northern Plains where rain was more abundant and cow numbers expanded by four percent, totaling about 170,000 cows.
facts.note: Last year is 2012; the article is dated February 2013 and the paragraph is about the 2012 drought.

facts.fact: Adjusted for buying power, income per person in China was 47% below India's in 1980 and 118% above it by 2013.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, China, India, the Food Transition, and Future Demand Growth (2015)
facts.quote: After adjusting for purchasing power parity, per capita income in China was 47% lower in 1980 than in India but 118% higher in 2013.

facts.fact: The Great Lakes and Plains states lost almost 45 percent of their farm jobs, about 630,000, from 1969 to 2021.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Changes in Farm Employment, 1969 to 2021 (2023)
facts.quote: Combined, the states in the Great Lakes and Plains regions lost almost 45 percent of their farm employment (roughly 630,000 jobs) since 1969.
facts.note: 2021 is the end year in the article's title.

facts.fact: US farm employment fell 35% from 1969 to 2021. In 1969 the Southeast alone held 31.6% of all farm jobs.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Changes in Farm Employment, 1969 to 2021 (2023)
facts.quote: Overall, U.S. farm employment has declined 35% percent since 1969. ... In 1969, the Southeast (31.6% of total U.S. farm employment), Plains (19.7%), and Great Lakes (16.3%) regions accounted for almost two-thirds of total U.S. farm employment.
facts.note: 2021 is the end year in the article's title.

facts.fact: Brazil's safrinha corn crop first topped 2 million metric tons in 1992/93. Its share of world corn grew elevenfold, from 0.45% to 5%.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Comparing Brazilian (1st and 2nd Crops), American, and Argentine Corn Yields (2022)
facts.quote: Safrinha corn in Brazil has grown significantly since 1992/93, when production exceeded 2 million metric tons for the first time. ... Safrinha share of world corn production increased eleven fold, from 0.45% to 5%.

facts.fact: In 1936 the Great Plains Committee told President Roosevelt about 15 million acres of the Dust Bowl region should go back to permanent grass.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Conservation Question, Part 2: Lessons Written in Dust (2019)
facts.quote: A 1936 report produced for President Franklin Roosevelt by the Great Plains Committee concluded that approximately 15 million acres in the region should be taken out of production and returned to permanent grassland (GPC Report 1936).

facts.fact: At its peak the Dust Bowl hit about 100 million acres, mostly in the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southwest Kansas, southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, The Conservation Question, Part 2: Lessons Written in Dust (2019)
facts.quote: the Dust Bowl has largely applied to the southern portion, concentrated in the Oklahoma and Texas panhandles, southwestern Kansas, southeastern Colorado and northeastern New Mexico (Stephens 1937). ... The peak of the Dust Bowl impacted about 100 million acres in this region (Egan 2006).

facts.fact: Federal marketing loans for crops date to 1938, and farmers generally repay them within 9 or 10 months.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, Farm Bill Review: Historical Background on Marketing Assistance Loans (2017)
facts.quote: If Congress reauthorizes the nonrecourse, price-support loan program in 2018 it will mark eighty years of this policy for U.S. commodity farmers. ... Also unlike the payment programs, farmers generally have to repay all or part of the loan within 9 or 10 months.
facts.note: 1938 is 2018 minus the eighty years stated on the page.

facts.fact: In mid-2024, heifers were nearly 40% of US cattle on feed, against 31% to 33% during most of the last herd expansion, a sign the herd was not rebuilding.
facts.source: University of Illinois farmdoc daily, How Big is the U.S. Cattle Herd? (2024)
facts.quote: the latter’s share of cattle on feed, as already mentioned, also remains similar to a year ago at nearly 40%, as compared to only 31%-33% during much of the last expansion. ... Hence, it appears the U.S. cattle industry overall remains in a contractionary phase
facts.note: Mid-2024 is the July 1, 2024 count the article discusses.

facts.fact: Nebraska, Colorado and Wyoming usually have the most US hailstorms. Where the three states meet, "hail alley," averages 7 to 9 hail days a year.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Nebraska, Colorado, and Wyoming usually have the most hailstorms. The area where these three states meet – “hail alley” – averages seven to nine hail days per year.
facts.note: seven to nine is written as 7 to 9.

facts.fact: Hail falls in paths called swaths. They can range from a few acres to an area 10 miles wide and 100 miles long.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: hail falls in paths known as hail swaths. ... They can range in size from a few acres to an area 10 miles wide and 100 miles long.

facts.fact: NSSL's expected hail fall speeds: 9 to 25 mph under 1 inch across, 25 to 40 mph for 1 to 1.75 inches, and 44 to 72 mph for 2 to 4 inches.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: For small hailstones (<1-inch in diameter), the expected fall speed is between 9 and 25 mph. For hailstones that one would typically see in a severe thunderstorm (1-inch to 1.75-inch in diameter), the expected fall speed is between 25 and 40 mph. In the strongest supercells that produce some of the largest hail one might expect to see (2-inches to 4-inches in diameter), the expected fall speed is between 44 and 72 mph.

facts.fact: Hail the size of a quarter, 1 inch across, is considered severe. A golf ball is 1 3/4 inches and a softball is 4 inches.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Quarter = 1 inch — hail quarter size or larger is considered severe ... Golf Ball = 1 3/4 inches ... Softball = 4 inches

facts.fact: Hailstones do not grow from being lofted to the top of a storm. Above that cold, below -40°F, all liquid water has frozen, and hailstones need liquid water to grow.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Hailstones also do not grow from being lofted to the top of the thunderstorm. At very high altitudes, the air is cold enough (below -40°F) that all liquid water will have frozen into ice, and hailstones need liquid water to grow to an appreciable size.

facts.fact: On April 4, 1977, both engines of a Southern Airways DC-9 ingested hail and lost thrust, and it crashed in New Hope, Georgia. 60 of the 81 passengers were killed, plus eight people on the ground.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: On April 4, 1977, a Southern Airways DC-9 crashed in New Hope, Georgia. Both engines of the plane ingested hail and lost thrust. ... Two of the four crew members and 60 of the 81 passengers were killed; eight others on the ground were also killed.

facts.fact: NSSL researchers developed the Hail Detection Algorithm, deployed in the late 1990s, the first operational hail sizing algorithm for the WSR-88D radars.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Hail Detection (page read 2026)
facts.quote: NSSL researchers developed the Hail Detection Algorithm, or HDA, which was the first operational hail sizing algorithm for the WSR-88D radars. Deployed in the late 1990s

facts.fact: About 1,200 tornadoes hit the US yearly, but official records date back only to 1950, so NSSL says the actual average number is not known.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: About 1,200 tornadoes hit the U.S. yearly. Since official tornado records only date back to 1950, we do not know the actual average number of tornadoes that occur each year.

facts.fact: Most tornadoes occur between 4 and 9 p.m. In the northern Plains and upper Midwest, tornado season is June or July.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: In the northern Plains and upper Midwest (North and South Dakota, Nebraska, Iowa, Minnesota), tornado season is in June or July. ... most tornadoes occur between 4–9 p.m.

facts.fact: As few as 20 percent of all supercell thunderstorms actually produce tornadoes.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado Types (page read 2026)
facts.quote: As few as 20 percent of all supercell thunderstorms actually produce tornadoes.

facts.fact: Nearly 20% of all tornadoes come from lines of strong thunderstorms, and they often occur in the late night and early morning hours.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado Types (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Nearly 20% of all tornadoes are associated with lines of strong thunderstorms called “quasi-linear convective systems” (QLCS). QLCS tornadoes frequently occur during the late night and early morning hours.

facts.fact: The strongest wind measured in a tornado, by mobile Doppler radar above ground level, was 318 mph on May 3, 1999, near Bridge Creek and Moore, Oklahoma.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Mobile Doppler radars can measure wind speeds in a tornado above ground level, and the strongest was 318 mph measured on May 3, 1999 near Bridge Creek/Moore, Oklahoma.

facts.fact: A tornado stays on the ground about five minutes on average, and a typical one travels at around 10 to 20 miles per hour.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: The average is about five minutes. ... A typical tornado travels at around 10–20 miles per hour.

facts.fact: There have been reports of tornadoes blowing dirt and creating a trench 3 feet deep, but it is very uncommon. Tornadoes have been known to strip asphalt pavement.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: There have been reports of tornadoes blowing dirt and creating a trench 3 feet deep, but it is very uncommon. Tornadoes have been known to strip asphalt pavement.

facts.fact: NSSL knows of one tornado reported in the Arctic Circle: in Inuvik, Northwest Territories, Canada, on July 15, 2012.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Are there tornadoes in the Arctic Circle? Not very many! ... However, we do know of one. There was a reported tornado in the city of Inuvik, NWT, Canada, on July 15, 2012.

facts.fact: In 2018, a wildfire near Redding, California, produced a supercell storm and a large, strong tornado that caused EF3 damage.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: 'Twisters' FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: In 2018, a wildfire near Redding, Cali., produced a supercell storm and eventually a large, strong tornado that caused EF3 damage to the surrounding communities.

facts.fact: For the most dangerous violent tornadoes, NSSL says "we're usually able to get tornado warnings out 15 to 20 minutes in advance."
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: 'Twisters' FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: especially for the most dangerous violent tornadoes, we’re usually able to get tornado warnings out 15 to 20 minutes in advance.

facts.fact: Any wind gust sustained for 3 seconds over 50 mph can cause damage to mobile homes, and straight-line winds can destroy an unanchored one as easily as a tornado.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Straight-line winds can also destroy a mobile home as easily as a tornado, especially one that is not anchored. Any wind gust that is sustained for 3 seconds over 50 mph can cause damage to mobile homes.

facts.fact: Damage from severe thunderstorm winds accounts for half of all severe reports in the lower 48 states and is more common than tornado damage.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Damaging Winds Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Damage from severe thunderstorm winds account for half of all severe reports in the lower 48 states and is more common than damage from tornadoes.

facts.fact: Even anchored mobile homes can be seriously damaged when winds gust over 80 mph.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Damaging Winds Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Even anchored mobile homes can be seriously damaged when winds gust over 80 mph.

facts.fact: A microburst is under 4 km across and lasts only five to 10 minutes, with maximum winds sometimes exceeding 100 mph.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Types of Damaging Winds (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Microbursts are small — less than 4 km across — and short-lived, lasting only five to 10 minutes, with maximum windspeeds sometimes exceeding 100 mph.

facts.fact: If a wind damage swath runs more than 240 miles with gusts of at least 58 mph along most of its length, the event may be classified as a derecho.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Types of Damaging Winds (page read 2026)
facts.quote: if the wind damage swath extends more than 240 miles (about 400 kilometers) and includes wind gusts of at least 58 mph (93 km/h) or greater along most of its length, then the event may be classified as a derecho.

facts.fact: The 58 mph severe wind limit dates to 1962, when negotiations with the Air Force raised the aviation watch minimum to 58 mph (50 knots). In 1970 the watches merged into one.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Damaging Winds FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Negotiations with the Air Force raised the minimum speed required for an aviation watch to 58 mph (50 knots) in 1962. In 1970, the Aviation Severe Thunderstorm and Public Severe Thunderstorm watches were combined into a single Severe Thunderstorm Watch

facts.fact: Worldwide there are an estimated 16 million thunderstorms a year, and roughly 2,000 are in progress at any given moment.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Thunderstorm Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Worldwide, there are an estimated 16 million thunderstorms each year, and at any given moment, there are roughly 2,000 thunderstorms in progress.

facts.fact: Lightning heats the air to around 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, much hotter than the surface of the sun, and that makes the air explode outward as thunder.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Energy from a lightning channel heats the air briefly to around 50,000 degrees Fahrenheit, much hotter than the surface of the sun. This causes the air to explode outward.

facts.fact: Count the seconds between a lightning flash and its thunder, then divide by 5 to get the distance in miles. Thunder can be heard up to 25 miles away.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Thunder can be heard up to 25 miles away from the lightning discharge ... Just count the number of seconds from the time you see a flash until you hear thunder. Sound travels approximately one fifth of a mile per second or one third of a kilometer per second, so dividing the number of seconds by 5 gives the number of miles to the flash

facts.fact: Across the continental US, an average of 20,000,000 cloud-to-ground flashes a year have been detected since 1989, striking at least 30 million points on the ground.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: an average of 20,000,000 cloud-to-ground flashes have been detected every year since the lightning detection network (NLDN) covered all of the continental US in 1989. In addition, about half of all flashes have more than one ground strike point, so at least 30 million points on the ground are struck on the average each year in the US.

facts.fact: According to the National Weather Service, the chance of an individual in the US being struck by lightning in a given year is one in 1.2 million. Over an 80-year lifetime it is 1 in 15,300.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: the chance of an individual in the U.S. being struck during a given year is one in 1.2 million. The odds of being struck in your lifetime (estimated to be 80 years) are 1 in 15,300.

facts.fact: A helmeted bicyclist was struck under a cloudless sky by a bolt thought to come from a thunderstorm about 16 km (roughly ten miles) away, hidden by mountains.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: A helmeted bicyclist experienced a lightning strike to the head under fair weather conditions with a cloudless sky. It was determined that the bolt probably originated in a thunderstorm that was about 16km (approximately ten miles) away and obscured by mountains.

facts.fact: Without thunderstorms and lightning, the electrical balance between the Earth and its atmosphere would disappear in 5 minutes.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Thunderstorm FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Without thunderstorms and lightning, the earth-atmosphere electrical balance would disappear in five minutes!
facts.note: five minutes is written as 5 minutes.

facts.fact: Sprites above a thunderstorm can extend up to 60 miles from the cloud top, and elves, discovered in 1992 by a Space Shuttle camera, can be up to 300 miles across.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning Types (page read 2026)
facts.quote: They can extend up to 60 miles from the cloud top. ... Elves are rapidly expanding disk-shaped regions of glowing that can be up to 300 miles across. ... Elves were discovered in 1992 by a low-light video camera on the Space Shuttle

facts.fact: A "bolt from the blue" starts inside a cloud, exits the side of the storm and travels horizontally before going to ground, so even a storm 6 miles away can be dangerous.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Lightning Types (page read 2026)
facts.quote: A “bolt from the blue” is a CG which starts inside a cloud, goes out the side of the storm, then travels horizontally away from the cloud before going to ground. ... So even a storm that is 6 miles away can be dangerous.

facts.fact: A creek only 6 inches deep in mountainous areas can swell to a 10-foot deep raging river in less than an hour if a thunderstorm lingers. Shallow, clayey soils let little water soak in.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Flood Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: Rocks and shallow, clayey soils do not allow much water to infiltrate into the ground. ... A creek only 6 inches deep in mountainous areas can swell to a 10-foot deep raging river in less than an hour

facts.fact: As little as 6 inches of fast moving water can sweep most any vehicle off a roadway, and the road bed under the water may be washed out.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Flood FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: As little as 6” of fast moving water can sweep most any vehicle off a roadway. Besides, you can't determine the condition of the road bed under the water. The road could be washed out

facts.fact: On July 31, 1976, a storm dumped a foot of rain into Colorado's Big Thompson Canyon, producing a raging torrent 19 feet high that caused 145 deaths.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Flood FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: On July 31, 1976, a storm in northern Colorado dumped a foot of rain into the Big Thompson Canyon producing a raging torrent of water 19 feet high and resulting in 145 deaths.

facts.fact: In 1964 the National Severe Storms Project moved to Norman, Oklahoma, and was reorganized as the National Severe Storms Laboratory with Edwin Kessler as director.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 1964 ... The entire National Severe Storms Project operation moves to Norman and is reorganized as the National Severe Storms Laboratory with Edwin Kessler as the new director.

facts.fact: On May 24, 1973, an NSSL team filmed a tornado's whole life cycle near its Doppler radar and found a pattern showing the tornado forming before it appeared on film: the Tornado Vortex Signature.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 1973 ... On May 24, an NSSL team intercepts a storm being scanned by the NSSL Doppler radar. The team documents the entire life cycle of the tornado on film. Researchers are able to compare the film images with Doppler radar data and discover a pattern that meant the tornado was forming before it appeared on film. They name this pattern the Tornado Vortex Signature (TVS).
facts.note: 1973 is the year heading above the May 24 entry.

facts.fact: The movie Twister was based on NSSL work in the mid-1980s with a 55-gallon drum of weather sensors called TOTO, which NSSL tried for several years to place in a tornado's path with minimal success.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado FAQ (page read 2026)
facts.quote: The movie Twister was based upon work NSSL did in the mid-1980s using a 55-gallon drum outfitted with various meteorological sensors. It was called TOTO (TOtable Tornado Observatory). NSSL tried for several years to put it in the path of an oncoming tornado, but had minimal success.

facts.fact: In 1985 NSSL researchers tested radar pulses sent both horizontally and vertically on the Cimarron radar and called the result dual-polarization technology.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 1985 ... NSSL researchers develop and test a technology that transmits radar energy pulses both horizontally and vertically on the Cimarron radar. They discover this capability provides valuable information about the type and amount of precipitation that is falling and call it dual-polarization technology.

facts.fact: In 2004 NSSL mosaicked all 130 National Weather Service and Department of Defense weather radars into the first real-time, coast-to-coast high-resolution picture of storms.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 2004 ... NSSL seamlessly mosaics all 130 NWS and Department of Defense weather radars across the U.S. to provide the first high-resolution depiction of storms and quantitative precipitation estimation products from coast-to-coast in real-time.

facts.fact: VORTEX2, begun in 2009, was the largest field tornado research project in history, with ten mobile radars and 40 other instrumented vehicles. It sampled 36 supercells and 11 tornadoes.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 2009 ... It is the largest field tornado research project in history deploying ten mobile radars and 40 other instrumented vehicles. ... sampling 36 supercell thunderstorms and 11 tornadoes.
facts.note: 2009 is the year heading above the VORTEX2 entry; 36 and 11 are from its 2010 entry.

facts.fact: In 2000, NSSL and the National Weather Service began publicly fighting the myth that highway overpasses are safe shelters in tornadoes.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 2000 ... NSSL and the NWS publicly fight the myth that highway overpasses are safe shelters in tornadoes.

facts.fact: In 2011 an NSSL algorithm helped alert a power company to the chance of a dust storm in Phoenix with 45 minutes of advance notice.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 2011 ... An NSSL algorithm helps alert a power company of the potential for a dust storm in Phoenix with 45 minutes advance notice.

facts.fact: In 2017 an NSSL researcher launched a weather balloon in the eye of a hurricane, which no one had done before, as part of efforts to collect data in the path of Hurricane Harvey.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, NSSL History (page read 2026)
facts.quote: 2017 ... A NSSL researcher manages to do what no one had done before — launch a weather balloon in the eye of a hurricane. The balloon launch is one part of NSSL's efforts to collect data in the path of Hurricane Harvey.

facts.fact: A wall cloud that may produce a tornado can exist for 10 to 20 minutes before a tornado appears, but not always.
facts.source: NOAA National Severe Storms Laboratory, Severe Weather 101: Tornado Basics (page read 2026)
facts.quote: A wall cloud that may produce a tornado can exist for 10–20 minutes before a tornado appears, but not always.

facts.fact: In 2022, US sales of grains and oilseeds totaled $168.7 billion, 31% of all US agriculture sales, and were up 58% from 2017.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, U.S. sales of grains and oilseeds totaled $168.7 billion, 31% of total U.S. agriculture sales. Sales of grains and oilseeds increased 58% from 2017 to 2022.

facts.fact: On farms specializing in grain and oilseeds, production costs in 2022 totaled $119.0 billion, up 40% from 2017. Fertilizer was the largest item at $23.2 billion, 19% of expenses.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: The production costs of farms that specialized in grain and oilseed production totaled $119.0 billion, up 40% from 2017. At $23.2 billion, fertilizer was the largest expense item, accounting for 19% of production expenses.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, corn was 29% of all US cropland harvested and soybeans were 28%. Illinois alone harvested 10 million acres of soybeans.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: Corn was 29% of all cropland harvested ... Soybeans were 28% of all cropland harvested; 10 million acres in Illinois.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, 5,120,561 acres of sorghum were harvested in the US, and Kansas and Texas harvested 74% of them.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: Sorghum 5,120,561 Sorghum Kansas and Texas harvested 74% of all acres.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022 Montana harvested 55% of all US dry edible pea acres, and North Dakota harvested 45% of all dry bean acres.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: Montana harvested 55% of all dry pea acres. ... North Dakota harvested 45% of all dry bean acres.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, 17 percent of all US farms specialized in grain and oilseeds, accounting for 32% of all agricultural land and 69% of harvested cropland.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Grain and Oilseed Production (2024)
facts.quote: Seventeen percent of all U.S. farms specialized in grain and oilseed production, accounting for 32% of all agricultural land and 69% of harvested cropland.
facts.note: Seventeen percent is written as 17 percent.

facts.fact: At $966 million in 2022 hog sales, Sampson County, North Carolina, had nearly 3% of US hog sales. Three of the top five hog counties were in Iowa.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Hogs and Pigs (2024)
facts.quote: At $966 million in 2022 hog sales, Sampson County, North Carolina, accounted for nearly 3% of U.S. hog sales. Three of the top five counties in hog sales, however, were in Iowa.

facts.fact: From 2002 to 2022, the share of US hogs on operations with fewer than 2,000 hogs fell from 25% to 5%, while the share on operations of 5,000 or more rose from 53% to 75%.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Hogs and Pigs (2024)
facts.quote: Between 2002 and 2022, the proportion of hogs on smaller operations (with fewer than 2,000 hogs) declined from 25% to 5%. The proportion on larger operations (5,000 hogs or more) increased from 53% to 75%.

facts.fact: US hog sales rose 38.4% to $36.4 billion from 2017 to 2022, while the number of farms with hog sales fell 13%, from 64,871 to 56,265.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Hogs and Pigs (2024)
facts.quote: U.S. hog sales totaled $36.4 billion, up 38.4% from 2017 ... the number of farms with sales of hogs decreased 13%, from 64,871 farms to 56,265 farms.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: On farms specializing in hogs, production costs in 2022 were $28.1 billion. Feed was the largest item at $13.5 billion, 48% of the total.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Hogs and Pigs (2024)
facts.quote: The production costs of farms specializing in hog and pig production totaled $28.1 billion, up 34% from 2017. The largest expense item was feed, which totaled $13.5 billion, or 48% of total production costs.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, broiler contractees were 73% of farms with broilers but 97% of production. For turkeys they were 36% of farms but 75% of production.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Poultry and Egg Production (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, broiler contractees accounted for 73% of the number of farms with broilers but 97% of production; for turkeys it was 36% of farms but 75% of production.

facts.fact: US farms sold 9.2 billion broiler and other meat-type chickens in 2022.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Poultry and Egg Production (2024)
facts.quote: 9.2 billion The number of broiler and other meat-type chickens sold in 2022.

facts.fact: From 2017 to 2022 the number of US farms selling milk fell 39%, from 40,336 to 24,470, while milk sales rose 44% to $52.8 billion.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Dairy Cattle and Milk Production (2024)
facts.quote: the number of farms with sales of milk from cows declined 39%, from 40,336 farms to 24,470 farms. Sales of milk from cows totaled $52.8 billion in 2022, up 44% from 2017.

facts.fact: California had 1.7 million milk cows at the end of 2022 and $9.7 billion in milk sales, the most of any state.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Dairy Cattle and Milk Production (2024)
facts.quote: California led the country in both milk cow inventory and sales, with 1.7 million milk cows at the end of 2022 and $9.7 billion in 2022 milk sales.

facts.fact: From 2017 to 2022, the share of US milk cows on operations with 2,500 or more cows rose from 35% to 45%, while operations under 1,000 cows fell from 45% to 35%.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Dairy Cattle and Milk Production (2024)
facts.quote: Between 2017 and 2022, the proportion of milk cows on smaller operations (with fewer than 1,000 milk cows) declined from 45% to 35%. The proportion on larger operations (2,500 milk cows or more) increased from 35% to 45%.

facts.fact: Every state raised and sold cattle in 2022, but Texas, Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa and Colorado made 57% of US cattle sales, $51 billion.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Cattle Production (2024)
facts.quote: Every state raised and sold cattle but the top five states – Texas, Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, and Colorado – accounted for 57% of the nation’s cattle sales in 2022 with $51 billion.

facts.fact: Nebraska had the largest fed cattle inventory at the end of 2022, 3 million head, 20% of all fed cattle.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Cattle Production (2024)
facts.quote: Nebraska had the largest fed cattle inventory with 3 million head, 20% of all fed cattle.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2023, 212,714 US farms irrigated 53.1 million acres with 81.0 million acre-feet of water. The number of irrigating farms fell 8.1% from 2018.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Irrigation and Water Management (2024)
facts.quote: In 2023, there were 212,714 farms in the United States that irrigated at some point during the year, an 8.1% decrease since 2018. They irrigated 53.1 million acres (about one-fourth of their farmland), applying 81.0 million acre-feet of water

facts.fact: An acre-foot of water is the amount needed to cover one acre one foot deep: 43,560 cubic feet, or 325,851 gallons.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Irrigation and Water Management (2024)
facts.quote: The amount of water required to cover one acre to a depth of one foot. This is equivalent to 43,560 cubic feet or 325,851 gallons.

facts.fact: In 2023, Arizona applied the most irrigation water per acre, an average of 4.3 acre-feet, while California applied the most in total, 22.6 million acre-feet.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Irrigation and Water Management (2024)
facts.quote: California applied the largest total amount of irrigation water, 22.6 million acrefeet. Arizona applied the most water per acre, an average of 4.3 acre-feet.
facts.note: 2023 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2023, 114,889 US farms used 456,058 wells for irrigation. The wells provided 54% of all water for open fields.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Irrigation and Water Management (2024)
facts.quote: In 2023, 114,889 U.S. farms used 456,058 wells for irrigation. The wells provided 54% of all water for open fields

facts.fact: In 2023, 3,597 free-flowing wells on 2,228 US farms did not need a pump to bring irrigation water to the surface.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Irrigation and Water Management (2024)
facts.quote: Most wells required dedicated pumps to move ground water to the surface, but 3,597 free-flowing wells on 2,228 farms did not require a pump.
facts.note: 2023 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, US sales of certified or exempt organic products were $9.6 billion, up 32% from 2017. California made 39% of the total.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Organic Agriculture (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, the United States reported $9.6 billion in sales of certified or exempt organic products, up 32% from 2017. ... California was again the top state for organic sales and accounted for 39% of the total value of certified organic agricultural products sold.

facts.fact: Monterey County, California, accounted for 8% of US organic sales in 2022, with $740 million.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Organic Agriculture (2024)
facts.quote: The top county, Monterey County, California, accounted for 8% of U.S. organic sales with $740 million.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: With $3.8 billion in vegetable sales in 2022, Monterey County, California, had more vegetable sales than any state except California.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Vegetable Production (2024)
facts.quote: With $3.8 billion in vegetable sales, Monterey County had more vegetable sales than any state except California.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, 69,452 US farms grew vegetables, down from 74,276 in 2017, while vegetable sales rose 44% to $28.2 billion.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Vegetable Production (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, of the 69,452 farms that produced vegetables ... The number of vegetable farms in 2017 was 74,276. ... U.S. vegetable sales (including melons) in 2022 were $28.2 billion, 5.2% of total U.S. agriculture sales. This was an increase of $8.6 billion, or 44%, since 2017

facts.fact: In 2023, crawfish were raised on 751 US aquaculture farms, with 97% in Louisiana.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Aquaculture (2024)
facts.quote: Crawfish, raised on 751 farms, 97% in Louisiana.
facts.note: 2023 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: Catfish sales were valued at $480 million in 2023, 59% of all US food fish sales. Trout accounted for 16%.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Aquaculture (2024)
facts.quote: Catfish sales, valued at $480 million in 2023, accounted for 59% of all food fish sales. Trout accounted for 16%.

facts.fact: Alligators accounted for $95 million in US aquaculture sales in 2023, 60% of miscellaneous aquaculture sales.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Aquaculture (2024)
facts.quote: Alligators accounted for $95 million in sales, 60% of total miscellaneous aquaculture sales in 2023.

facts.fact: In 2022, 95% of US farms were family-owned. Large-scale family farms were 4% of all farms but produced 51% of the value of all agricultural products.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Family Farms (2025)
facts.quote: In 2022, 95% of U.S. farms were family-owned. ... Large-scale family farms made up 4% of all U.S. farms, but produced 51% of the value of all agricultural products.

facts.fact: Since 1974, the Census of Agriculture has defined a farm as any place from which $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farms and Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: Since 1974, the Census of Agriculture has defined a farm as any place from which $1,000 or more of agricultural products were produced and sold, or normally would have been sold, during the census year.

facts.fact: With nearly 231,000 farms in 2022, Texas had more than twice as many farms as the next state.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farms and Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: With nearly 231,000 farms, Texas had more than twice as many farms as the next state.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2022, about 9 out of 10 acres of agricultural land were permanent pasture or cropland. Woodland made up 8% of farmland and the other 4% was farmsteads, buildings and livestock facilities.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farms and Farmland (2024)
facts.quote: Approximately nine out of 10 acres of agricultural land in 2022 were either permanent pasture or cropland. Woodland accounted for 8% of farmland, and the remaining 4% included land in farmsteads, buildings, livestock facilities, etc.
facts.note: nine out of 10 is written as 9 out of 10.

facts.fact: In 2022, Fresno County, California, had larger agriculture sales than 23 individual states.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farm Economics (2024)
facts.quote: the top county, Fresno, had larger agriculture sales than 23 individual states.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: At the farm level, average income in 2022 was $79,790, up 85%, or almost double, from 2017.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farm Economics (2024)
facts.quote: At the farm level, average income in 2022 was $79,790, up 85% or almost double from 2017.

facts.fact: In 2022 the top five commodities accounted for $363 billion in sales, 67% of all US agriculture sales. Cattle and calves ranked first at $89.4 billion.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farm Economics (2024)
facts.quote: Cattle and calves was the top ranked commodity, with $89.4 billion in sales. ... The top five commodities accounted for $363 billion in sales, 67% of U.S. total agriculture sales.
facts.note: 2022 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 2025, livestock farm expenditures ($255 billion) exceeded crop farm expenditures ($235.3 billion) for the first time since 2015.
facts.source: USDA NASS, U.S. Farm Production Expenditures, 2025 (2026)
facts.quote: In 2025, livestock farm expenditures ($255 billion) exceeded crop farm expenditures ($235.3 billion) for the first time since 2015.

facts.fact: In 2024, more than 2 million landowners rented out 347.8 million acres for agricultural purposes. 13% were operating landlords and 87% did not operate farms.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: Farmland Ownership and Tenure, 2024 TOTAL Survey (2026)
facts.quote: In 2024, more than 2 million landowners rented out 347.8 million acres of land for agricultural purposes. Of these landowners, 13% were farmers who owned and operated farms and ranches as well as rented out farmland (operating landlords) and 87% were landlords who do not operate farms (non-operating landlords).

facts.fact: In 2022 the US had 1,011,715 producers who had farmed for 10 or fewer years, 30% of 3.37 million producers. Their average age was 47.1, against 58.1 for all farmers.
facts.source: USDA NASS, 2022 Census of Agriculture Highlights: New and Beginning Producers (2024)
facts.quote: In 2022, the United States had 1,011,715 producers who identified as beginning farmers. A beginning farmer is anyone who has farmed for 10 or fewer years. They accounted for 30% of the country’s 3.37 million producers. ... The average age of a beginning farmer was 47.1, much younger than the average age of all farmers (58.1).

facts.fact: In NASS's 2025 conservation survey, 83.7% of respondents reported using conservation practices, but only 31.7% of those reported having a written conservation plan.
facts.source: USDA NASS, Conservation Effects Assessment Project, 2025 (2026)
facts.quote: About 83.7% of survey respondents reported using conservation practices. Of those survey respondents, 31.7% reported having a written conservation plan.
facts.note: 2025 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: Of the 87.9% of respondents who used fertilizers in NASS's 2025 survey, 73.5% named fertilizer costs as a decision factor and 65.9% named a nutrient management plan.
facts.source: USDA NASS, Conservation Effects Assessment Project, 2025 (2026)
facts.quote: Of the 87.9% of survey respondents who reported using fertilizers, the two most common decision factors were fertilizer costs and nutrient management plans. ... Fertilizer costs 73.5% Nutrient management plan 65.9%
facts.note: 2025 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In NASS's 2025 conservation survey, 60.3% of respondents used no-till or minimum tillage to manage pests, the most common pest practice, applied to 73.2% of the cropland surveyed.
facts.source: USDA NASS, Conservation Effects Assessment Project, 2025 (2026)
facts.quote: no-till or minimum tillage to manage pests were the most common practices reported. Of the survey respondents who reported using pest management practices, no-till or minimum tillage practices to manage pests were applied to 73.2% of the cropland surveyed. ... 60.3% No-till/minimum to manage pests
facts.note: 2025 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: On Thanksgiving, Americans averaged 128 minutes of meal preparation and cleanup in 2003 to 2015 surveys, over three times the 34 minutes on an average weekend day.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Yes, Thanksgiving really is a day of cooking (2016)
facts.quote: On this national holiday over a survey period of 2003-15, Americans spent an average of 128 minutes in meal preparation and cleanup—over three times the 34 minutes spent on these tasks on an average Saturday or Sunday.
facts.note: 2015 is the year the source page reports for this figure (from its title, date or text), not a count in the quote.

facts.fact: In 1988 pollination was only 11 percent of beekeeper revenue. By 2016 it was 41 percent, slightly more than honey sales, mainly because of the growth in almond acreage.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Almond pollination service fees more than doubled since 2004 (2018)
facts.quote: As late as 1988, pollination services accounted for only 11 percent of beekeeper revenue, with the majority of revenue coming from honey sales. In 2016, that share had risen to 41 percent, slightly surpassing revenue from honey sales. The relatively recent increase in pollination service revenue mainly stems from the dramatic growth in acreage for almonds.

facts.fact: Almond farmers paid $165 per honey bee colony rented in 2016, roughly triple the average of $55 paid for other crops.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Almond pollination service fees more than doubled since 2004 (2018)
facts.quote: Recent data show almond farmers paid $165 per colony rented in 2016, roughly triple the average of $55 for other crops.

facts.fact: National average corn yield stood near 30 bushels per acre from the 1860s, when USDA began measuring, through the 1930s, and reached nearly 180 bushels per acre by the 2010s.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Technological innovations have increased corn yields (2017)
facts.quote: Average national corn yield (a productivity measure) rose from around 30 bushels per acre in the 1930s (where it stood since USDA began measuring them in the 1860s) to nearly 180 bushels per acre in the present decade.
facts.note: The present decade, for a chart dated 2017, is the 2010s.

facts.fact: The US food supply provided 21.9 pounds of frozen dairy products per person in 2014, down from 26.2 pounds 40 years earlier. Ice cream was 84 percent of the total.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Availability of frozen dairy products was 22 pounds per American in 2014 (2017)
facts.quote: the food supply provided 21.9 pounds of frozen dairy products per person in 2014—a decline from 26.2 pounds per person 40 years ago. Ice cream (regular, low fat, and nonfat) is still America’s favorite frozen dairy treat, accounting for 84 percent of total frozen dairy product availability.

facts.fact: In 2017 the US had 36,555 food and beverage processing plants employing more than 1.7 million people. California had 5,731 of them, including 1,499 wineries.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: California, New York, and Texas rank as the top 3 States in number of U.S. food and beverage processing plants (2020)
facts.quote: In 2017, there were 36,555 food and beverage processing plants located throughout the United States, employing more than 1.7 million people. ... California had the most plants (5,731) ... wineries (1,499 plants)

facts.fact: The number of US ethanol plants more than quadrupled since 1999. As of 2016, plants ran at roughly 97 percent of capacity, producing over 15 billion gallons.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: U.S. ethanol plants are operating near full capacity but constraints limit growth (2018)
facts.quote: The number of U.S. ethanol plants more than quadrupled since 1999 ... As of 2016, existing plants were operating at roughly 97 percent of total capacity, translating to over 15 billion gallons of ethanol produced.

facts.fact: Americans consumed an average of 156.3 pounds of fresh and processed vegetables per person in 2015. Potatoes led at 48.3 pounds and tomatoes were second at 28.3 pounds.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Potatoes and tomatoes are America’s top vegetable choices (2018)
facts.quote: Americans consumed an average of 156.3 pounds of fresh and processed vegetables per person in 2015. ... Potatoes claimed the #1 spot at 48.3 pounds per person ... total tomato consumption—fresh and canned—came in second at 28.3 pounds per person.

facts.fact: Loss-adjusted daily calories per American fell 2 percent from 2000 to 2010, from 2,545 to 2,481. Plant-based foods supplied 70 percent in both years.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Seventy percent of U.S. calories consumed in 2010 were from plant-based foods (2017)
facts.quote: Loss-adjusted daily calories per person decreased by 2 percent between 2000 and 2010 from 2,545 to 2,481 calories. The share of calories from animal- and plant-based foods was the same in both years at 30 percent and 70 percent, respectively.

facts.fact: Caloric sweeteners available per American peaked at 153.1 pounds in 1999 and fell to 131.0 pounds in 2014. Corn sweeteners fell from 85.2 pounds to 60.7 pounds.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Availability of refined sugars has been higher than corn sweeteners since 2011 (2016)
facts.quote: In 2014, 131.0 pounds per person of caloric sweeteners were available for consumption by U.S. consumers, down from a high of 153.1 pounds per person in 1999. Availability of total corn sweeteners (high-fructose corn syrup (HFCS), glucose syrup, and dextrose) contributed to the drop, falling from its peak of 85.2 pounds per person in 1999 to 60.7 pounds per person in 2014.

facts.fact: In 2014, 5.4 percent of US farm operators reported owning oil and gas rights. In counties with oil and gas production the share was 11.4 percent.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Ownership of oil and gas rights among farm operators varies across States (2018)
facts.quote: Nationally, 5.4 percent of farm operators reported owning oil and gas rights in 2014. In counties with oil and gas production, the share was higher at 11.4 percent.

facts.fact: Fresh and frozen shellfish reached 5.3 pounds per American in 2016, more than double 1970, passing canned tuna in 1991. Canned tuna fell to 2.1 pounds from almost 4 pounds in 1989.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: U.S. shellfish availability more than doubled from 1970 to 2016 (2019)
facts.quote: fresh and frozen shellfish at 5.3 pounds per person, which more than doubled since 1970. ... surpassing canned tuna in 1991. The third highest seafood product, canned tuna, fell to 2.1 pounds per person in 2016 after reaching almost 4 pounds per person in 1989.

facts.fact: From 1993 to 2017, real farm debt rose 87 percent, to levels near the peaks of the late 1970s and early 1980s.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Farm sector debt at 30-year high, but interest expenses remain low (2019)
facts.quote: Farm sector debt has reached levels near the peak levels of the late 1970s and early 1980s. ... From 1993 to 2017, real (inflation-adjusted) farm debt increased by 87 percent, or 4 percent per year on average.

facts.fact: The midpoint corn acreage, where half of the acres are on farms harvesting more and half on farms harvesting less, rose from 200 acres in 1987 to 685 acres in 2017.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Agricultural consolidation has increased the midpoint acreage for most crops since 1987 (2020)
facts.quote: In 1987, for example, the midpoint acreage for corn was 200 acres; it increased to 685 acres by 2017.

facts.fact: US agriculture emitted 698 million metric tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent in 2018: 12.3 percent as carbon dioxide, 36.2 percent as methane and 51.3 percent as nitrous oxide.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Agriculture contributed 10.5 percent of U.S. greenhouse gas emissions in 2018 (2020)
facts.quote: U.S. agriculture emitted 698 million metric tons of carbon-dioxide equivalent in 2018: 12.3 percent as carbon dioxide, 36.2 percent as methane, and 51.3 percent as nitrous oxide.

facts.fact: Citrus greening (HLB) has attacked the US citrus industry since 2005, and ERS says it is estimated to have infected all groves in Florida. The 2018/19 US citrus crop was valued at $3.35 billion.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Citrus Greening Disease caused falling production in Florida, but production is forecast to stabilize in 2019/20 (2020)
facts.quote: The United States is a major global citrus producer with the 2018/19 crop valued at $3.35 billion. ... including Huanglongbing (HLB), which has attacked the industry since 2005. ... it is now estimated to have infected all groves in the State.

facts.fact: US avocado consumption tripled from 2001 to 8 pounds per person in 2018. California grew 93 percent of 2018 US output and Mexico supplied 89 percent of fresh avocado imports.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: U.S. avocado demand is climbing steadily (2020)
facts.quote: Per capita consumption of avocados has tripled since 2001 to 8 pounds per person in 2018. ... California the major producer, accounting for 93 percent of U.S. avocado output in that year. ... by 2018 accounted for 89 percent of fresh avocado imports.

facts.fact: US agricultural exports grew from $46.1 billion in 1994 to $136.7 billion in 2019. China's share rose from 3 percent in 1994 to 2000 to 14 percent in 2010 to 2019.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Destinations of U.S. agricultural exports have shifted over last quarter century (2020)
facts.quote: U.S. agricultural exports have grown significantly over the last quarter century, from $46.1 billion in 1994 to $136.7 billion in 2019. ... whose share of U.S. agricultural exports more than quadrupled from 3 percent during 1994-2000 to 14 percent during 2010-19.

facts.fact: Cover crop use on US cropland increased 50 percent between 2012 and 2017. Persistent use occurred on 69 percent of cotton acres and 56 percent of corn-for-silage acres.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Cover crop use is more persistent on cotton and corn silage fields (2021)
facts.quote: The use of cover crops on U.S. cropland increased 50 percent between 2012 and 2017, according to data in the U.S. Census of Agriculture. ... persistent cover crop use occurred on 69 percent of cotton acres (2015), 56 percent of corn-for-silage acres (2016)

facts.fact: In 2019 Americans ate 12.1 pounds of regular ice cream each, about 4 pounds, or 25 percent, less than in 2000.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: U.S. residents scooped more ice cream in 2000 than in 2019 (2021)
facts.quote: Consumption of regular ice cream in 2019 totaled 12.1 pounds per person, a decrease of about 4 pounds, or 25 percent, from 2000.

facts.fact: The Federal Government provides 64 percent of public agricultural research and development funding in the US. States and other sources provide the other 36 percent.
facts.source: USDA Economic Research Service, Charts of Note: Federal Government is primary funder of U.S. agricultural research and development (2022)
facts.quote: The Federal Government provides 64 percent of public agricultural research and development (R&D) funding in the United States. State governments and non-governmental sources, including funds generated by the universities themselves, account for the other 36 percent of funds for public agricultural R&D.
